lessons.title: Understanding Limits
lessons.description: Explore what limits are and why they matter for calculus.
lessons.formula:
lim(x→c) f(x) = L

If f(x) → L as x → c from both sides
lessons.content:
A limit describes the value a function approaches as the input approaches a specific value. It is the foundational concept of all calculus. When we write lim(x→c) f(x) = L, we mean that f(x) gets arbitrarily close to L as x gets close to c.

Limits can be approached from the left (x→c⁻), from the right (x→c⁺), or both sides. For the two-sided limit to exist, both one-sided limits must exist and be equal.

Indeterminate forms like 0/0 and ∞/∞ require special techniques such as factoring, rationalizing, or L'Hôpital's Rule to evaluate.
steps: Plug in the value directly
If 0/0 or indeterminate, try factoring
Try rationalizing the numerator or denominator
Check one-sided limits for piecewise functions
If infinite, describe the behavior

examples.title: Direct Substitution
examples.text: lim(x→3) (x²+2x) = 9+6 = 15. Direct substitution works because the function is continuous at x=3.

examples.title: Factoring Method
examples.text: lim(x→2) (x²−4)/(x−2) = lim(x→2) (x+2)(x−2)/(x−2) = lim(x→2) (x+2) = 4. Cancel the common factor first.

lessons.tip: Always try direct substitution first! If you get 0/0 or ∞/∞, that's your signal to use algebra to simplify before trying again.

quiz.explanation: Direct substitution: 3(5)−1 = 14.

quiz.q: If lim(x→c⁻) f(x) ≠ lim(x→c⁺) f(x), then:
quiz.explanation: Both one-sided limits must agree for the two-sided limit to exist.
This is a fundamental trigonometric limit proven by the squeeze theorem.

lessons.title: One-Sided Limits
lessons.description: Evaluate limits from the left and right side of a point.
lessons.formula:
lim(x→c⁻) f(x) = left-hand limit
lim(x→c⁺) f(x) = right-hand limit

Two-sided limit exists if BOTH are equal
lessons.content:
One-sided limits tell us what happens when we approach a point from one direction only. The left-hand limit lim(x→c⁻) means x approaches c from values less than c. The right-hand limit lim(x→c⁺) means x approaches c from values greater than c.

For the two-sided limit to exist, both one-sided limits must exist and be equal. If they differ, we have a jump discontinuity.

Piecewise functions are the most common scenario where one-sided limits differ at the boundary points between pieces.
steps: Identify the point c you are approaching
Check the function definition for x < c (left approach)
Check the function definition for x > c (right approach)
Evaluate both limits
Compare: if equal, the limit exists; if not, the limit DNE

examples.title: Piecewise Function
examples.text: f(x) = x+1 for x<2, and 2x for x≥2. lim(x→2⁻) f(x) = 3, lim(x→2⁺) f(x) = 4. Since 3≠4, lim(x→2) f(x) DNE.

examples.title: Absolute Value
examples.text: lim(x→0⁻) |x|/x = −1, lim(x→0⁺) |x|/x = 1. The left and right limits disagree, so the limit does not exist at 0.

lessons.tip: For absolute value functions, always split into two cases (positive and negative) to evaluate one-sided limits separately.

quiz.q: f(x)=x² for x<1, f(x)=x+2 for x≥1. lim(x→1⁻) f(x) = ?
quiz.explanation: From the left: use x², so lim(x→1⁻) x² = 1.
From the right: use x+2, so lim(x→1⁺) (x+2) = 3.
Left limit (1) ≠ right limit (3), so the two-sided limit does not exist.
As x approaches 0 from the positive side, 1/x grows without bound.

lessons.title: Infinite Limits & Vertical Asymptotes
lessons.description: Understand when limits approach infinity and identify vertical asymptotes.
lessons.formula:
lim(x→c) f(x) = +∞ if f(x) grows without bound
lim(x→c) f(x) = −∞ if f(x) decreases without bound

Vertical asymptote at x = c when lim = ±∞
lessons.content:
Infinite limits occur when a function grows or decreases without bound as x approaches a certain value. When lim(x→c) f(x) = ±∞, the line x = c is a vertical asymptote.

For rational functions f(x)/g(x), vertical asymptotes occur where the denominator equals zero but the numerator does not. If both numerator and denominator are zero at x=c, you must factor and simplify first.

One-sided infinite limits can differ: for example, lim(x→0⁺) 1/x = +∞ but lim(x→0⁻) 1/x = −∞. The vertical asymptote still exists at x=0.
steps: Set the denominator equal to zero to find candidate asymptotes
Check if numerator also equals zero at that point
If not, the vertical asymptote exists at that point
If yes, factor and simplify — the asymptote may be a hole instead
Check one-sided limits for sign changes

examples.title: Finding Vertical Asymptotes
examples.text: f(x) = 1/(x−3)². Denominator zero at x=3, numerator nonzero. Vertical asymptote at x=3. Both one-sided limits are +∞.

examples.title: Rational Function
examples.text: f(x) = (x+1)/(x²−4) = (x+1)/((x−2)(x+2)). Vertical asymptotes at x=2 and x=−2.

lessons.tip: A vertical asymptote at x=c means the function's graph has an invisible vertical wall that it approaches but never touches.

quiz.explanation: Denominator zero at x=−5, numerator nonzero → vertical asymptote.
x−3 approaches 0⁺, so 1/(tiny positive) → +∞.
x−3 approaches 0⁻, so 1/(tiny negative) → −∞.
Factor: (x−3)(x+3)/(x−3) = x+3 for x≠3. This is a removable hole, not an asymptote.

lessons.title: Continuity & the Intermediate Value Theorem
lessons.description: Determine if functions are continuous and apply the IVT.
lessons.formula:
Continuity at x=a requires:
1. f(a) is defined
2. lim(x→a) f(x) exists
3. lim(x→a) f(x) = f(a)

IVT: If f continuous on [a,b] and f(a)·f(b)<0, then f(c)=0 for some c in (a,b).
lessons.content:
A function is continuous at a point if you can draw the graph through that point without lifting your pencil. Three conditions must all hold: the function must be defined at the point, the limit must exist, and the limit must equal the function value.

Discontinuities are classified as removable (a hole), jump (the function leaps), or infinite (vertical asymptote). Each type has a different cause and behavior.

The Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees that a continuous function on a closed interval takes on every value between its endpoints. This is essential for proving roots exist and is the basis for numerical methods like bisection.
steps: Check f(a) is defined
Check the two-sided limit exists
Verify limit = function value
Classify any discontinuities by type
Apply IVT when given values with opposite signs

examples.title: IVT to Prove a Root
examples.text: f(x) = x³+x−1. f(0)=−1, f(1)=1. Since f is continuous and changes sign on [0,1], there exists c in (0,1) where f(c)=0.

examples.title: Classifying Discontinuity
examples.text: f(x) = sin(x)/x at x=0: f(0) undefined → discontinuous. But lim(x→0) sin(x)/x = 1, so it's removable.

lessons.tip: Use IVT like a detective: if you can show a function is continuous and takes values of opposite sign at two points, a root must exist somewhere between them!

quiz.q: f(x) = x²−1. By IVT, on [0,2], f takes the value:
quiz.explanation: f(0)=−1, f(2)=3. By IVT, f takes every value from −1 to 3 on [0,2].

quiz.q: A function with a hole has what type of discontinuity?
quiz.explanation: A hole is a removable discontinuity because you can 'fill in' the single point.

options: Function to be continuous on a closed interval
quiz.explanation: IVT requires continuity on a closed interval [a,b].

quiz.q: f(x) = 1/x is discontinuous at x=0. What type?
quiz.explanation: 1/x has a vertical asymptote at x=0, making it an infinite discontinuity.

lessons.title: Evaluating Limits with Algebraic Methods
lessons.description: Use factoring, rationalizing, and special limits to evaluate tricky limits.
lessons.formula:
Key limits:
lim(x→0) sin(x)/x = 1
lim(x→0) (1−cos x)/x = 0
lim(x→∞) (1+1/x)^x = e

L'Hôpital: if 0/0 or ∞/∞, lim f/g = lim f'/g'
lessons.content:
When direct substitution gives an indeterminate form like 0/0, you need algebraic techniques to evaluate the limit. Common methods include factoring, rationalizing, dividing by the highest power, and using special known limits.

L'Hôpital's Rule applies when you have 0/0 or ∞/∞: take the derivative of the numerator and denominator separately, then re-evaluate the limit. This can be applied repeatedly if needed.

Special trigonometric limits like lim(x→0) sin(x)/x = 1 and lim(x→0) (1−cos x)/x = 0 are essential building blocks for derivative proofs later.
steps: Try direct substitution first
If 0/0: try factoring out common terms
If radicals: try multiplying by the conjugate
If ∞/∞: divide by highest power of x
If still indeterminate: apply L'Hôpital's Rule

examples.title: L'Hôpital's Rule
examples.text: lim(x→0) (e^x−1)/x → 0/0. Apply L'Hôpital: lim(x→0) e^x/1 = 1.

lessons.tip: L'Hôpital's Rule is a power tool — but only for 0/0 or ∞/∞ forms. Never apply it to other limit forms!

quiz.explanation: 0/0 form. By L'Hôpital: derivative of e^x is e^x, derivative of x is 1. So lim = e^0/1 = 1.
This is a fundamental trigonometric limit value that must be memorized.

quiz.q: L'Hôpital's Rule applies when the limit form is:
quiz.explanation: L'Hôpital's Rule only works for 0/0 and ∞/∞ indeterminate forms directly.
Divide all terms by x²: (3+2/x)/(1+1/x²) → 3/1 = 3.

lessons.title: Limit Properties & The Squeeze Theorem
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of limit properties & the squeeze theorem
lessons.formula:
Limit Laws:
  lim[f(x) + g(x)] = lim f(x) + lim g(x)
  lim[f(x) * g(x)] = lim f(x) * lim g(x)
  lim[f(x) / g(x)] = lim f(x) / lim g(x), if lim g(x) != 0

Squeeze Theorem:
  If g(x) <= f(x) <= h(x) near a, and
  lim g(x) = L = lim h(x), then lim f(x) = L.

Power rule: lim [f(x)]^n = [lim f(x)]^n
Root rule:  lim n-th-root(f(x)) = n-th-root(lim f(x))
lessons.content:
Limit properties (limit laws) let you evaluate complex limits by breaking them into simpler parts. The sum, difference, product, and quotient rules mirror the familiar arithmetic operations. The power rule states that lim[f(x)]^n = [lim f(x)]^n, and the root rule extends this to radicals. These laws apply only when the individual limits exist (and the denominator is nonzero for quotients).

The Squeeze Theorem (Sandwich Theorem) handles cases where direct substitution fails. If you can bound a function between two others that share the same limit at a point, the trapped function must converge to that same limit. A classic example is proving lim(x->0) x sin(1/x) = 0: since −|x| ≤ x sin(1/x) ≤ |x| and both bounds go to 0, the limit is 0.

Combined with algebraic manipulation (factoring, rationalizing, trigonometric identities), the limit laws and Squeeze Theorem resolve the vast majority of limit problems encountered in calculus without requiring the full epsilon-delta definition.
steps: Attempt direct substitution first; if it yields 0/0 or undefined, proceed to algebraic techniques
For Squeeze Theorem problems, find two bounding functions g(x) and h(x) that are easy to evaluate
Verify that g(x) <= f(x) <= h(x) in a deleted neighborhood of the limit point
Compute lim g(x) and lim h(x); they must be equal to the same value L
Conclude by the Squeeze Theorem that lim f(x) = L

examples.title: Squeeze Theorem: lim(x->0) x^2 * sin(1/x)
examples.text:
Evaluate lim(x->0) of x^2 * sin(1/x).

Since -1 <= sin(1/x) <= 1 for all x != 0:
-x^2 <= x^2 * sin(1/x) <= x^2

Both bounds: lim(x->0)(-x^2) = 0 and lim(x->0)(x^2) = 0.

By the Squeeze Theorem: lim(x->0) x^2 * sin(1/x) = 0.

Note: direct substitution fails because sin(1/0) is undefined.

examples.title: Using Limit Laws
examples.text:
Evaluate lim(x->3) of (x^2 + 2x - 1) / (x - 1).

By the limit laws:
Numerator: lim(x->3)(x^2 + 2x - 1) = 9 + 6 - 1 = 14
Denominator: lim(x->3)(x - 1) = 2 (nonzero, so quotient rule applies)

lim(x->3) (x^2 + 2x - 1)/(x - 1) = 14/2 = 7.

Verify: f(3) = (9+6-1)/(3-1) = 14/2 = 7. Matches!

lessons.tip: When using the Squeeze Theorem, a reliable strategy is to multiply your function by -1 and +1 to create bounds. For f(x) * sin(something), use -|f(x)| <= f(x)*sin <= |f(x)|.

quiz.q: Evaluate lim(x->0) x^3 * cos(1/x) using the Squeeze Theorem.
quiz.explanation: -|x^3| <= x^3*cos(1/x) <= |x^3|, and both bounds go to 0, so the limit is 0.

quiz.q: Which condition is NOT required for the Squeeze Theorem?
options: f(x) must be differentiable at a
g, f, h must all be defined near a (except possibly at a)
quiz.explanation: The Squeeze Theorem does not require differentiability, only that the bounds squeeze f to the same limit.

quiz.q: Using limit laws, find lim(x->2) [3x^2 - x + 4].
quiz.explanation: 3(4) - 2 + 4 = 12 - 2 + 4 = 14. Direct substitution works because the function is a polynomial.

quiz.q: The quotient rule for limits requires that:
quiz.explanation: lim[f/g] = lim f / lim g only when lim g(x) != 0 to avoid division by zero.

lessons.title: Intermediate Value Theorem Applications
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of intermediate value theorem applications
lessons.formula:
Intermediate Value Theorem:
  If f is continuous on [a, b] and N is between
  f(a) and f(b), then there exists c in (a, b)
  such that f(c) = N.

Bisection method approximation:
  midpoint = (a + b) / 2
  If f(a)*f(mid) < 0, root is in [a, mid]
  If f(mid)*f(b) < 0, root is in [mid, b]

Error bound after n bisections:
  |c - midpoint| < (b - a) / 2^n
lessons.content:
The Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT) guarantees that a continuous function on a closed interval [a, b] takes on every value between f(a) and f(b). The most important application is proving that a root exists: if f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs (i.e., f(a)·f(b) < 0), then f(c) = 0 for some c ∈ (a, b). This is a pure existence result—it tells you a root is there, but not exactly where.

The bisection method exploits the IVT numerically: repeatedly halve the interval and keep the half where the sign change occurs. Each step reduces the interval width by half, so after n bisections the root is known within (b−a)/2^n. For example, starting with [1, 2] and bisecting 10 times locates the root to within 1/1024 ≈ 0.001.

The IVT also applies to proving that equations have solutions (showing a continuous function crosses a target value) and to demonstrating that certain numbers are attainable. It cannot be used if the function is discontinuous or if the domain is open.
steps: Verify that f is continuous on the closed interval [a, b]
Compute f(a) and f(b) and check they have opposite signs (or that N is between them)
If f(a)*f(b) < 0, conclude by IVT that a root c exists in (a, b)
Apply bisection: compute midpoint m = (a+b)/2, evaluate f(m), and select the subinterval with the sign change
Repeat until the interval width is within your desired tolerance

examples.title: Proving a Root Exists
examples.text:
Show that f(x) = x^3 - x - 2 has a root in the interval [1, 2].

f(1) = 1 - 1 - 2 = -2
f(2) = 8 - 2 - 2 = 4

f is a polynomial, so it is continuous everywhere. Since f(1) = -2 < 0 and f(2) = 4 > 0, and f(1)*f(2) = -8 < 0, by IVT there exists c in (1, 2) such that f(c) = 0.

The actual root is x = 1.5214...

lessons.tip: The IVT only guarantees existence, not uniqueness. A function can cross zero multiple times in an interval. To prove uniqueness, you need additional information such as monotonicity (the function is strictly increasing or decreasing).

quiz.q: Can the IVT prove that f(x) = x^2 has a root on [-1, 2]?
options: No, because f(-1) and f(2) are both positive
No, because x^2 is not continuous
quiz.explanation: f(-1) = 1 > 0 and f(2) = 4 > 0. There is no sign change, so IVT cannot guarantee a root here.

quiz.q: After 10 bisection steps starting from [0, 1], what is the maximum error?
Why does the IVT require continuity?
options: It does not actually require continuity
A discontinuous function could jump over the target value
Only polynomials are covered by IVT
Continuity makes the proof simpler but is not necessary
quiz.explanation: A discontinuous function with a jump discontinuity could skip values between f(a) and f(b), violating the theorem.

quiz.q: f(x) = e^x - 3 on [0, 2]: f(0) = -2, f(2) = 4.38. What does IVT tell us?
options: There is at least one root in (0, 2)
quiz.explanation: IVT guarantees at least one c in (0,2) where e^c = 3. (Actual root: ln3 = 1.099.)

lessons.title: Differentiability vs Continuity
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of differentiability vs continuity
lessons.formula:
Derivative (definition):
  f'(a) = lim(h->0) [f(a+h) - f(a)] / h

Key theorem:
  Differentiable => Continuous
  (but NOT conversely)

Left-hand derivative:
  f'_(a) = lim(h->0-) [f(a+h) - f(a)] / h

Right-hand derivative:
  f'+(a) = lim(h->0+) [f(a+h) - f(a)] / h

f'(a) exists iff f'_(a) = f'+(a)
lessons.content:
Differentiability means a function has a well-defined tangent at every point—the derivative limit exists. A fundamental theorem states: if f is differentiable at a, then f is continuous at a. The converse is false: |x| is continuous at 0 but not differentiable there because the left-hand derivative (−1) does not equal the right-hand derivative (+1). This creates a "corner" or cusp.

Common reasons a continuous function fails to be differentiable include: sharp corners (like |x| at 0), vertical tangents (like x^{1/3} at 0, where the derivative limit approaches infinity), and discontinuities (the function itself is not continuous). To test differentiability at a point, compute both the left-hand and right-hand derivative limits and check if they agree.

Higher differentiability (f being twice differentiable, C^2, C^inf) implies progressively smoother behavior. Polynomials are C^inf (infinitely differentiable everywhere), while functions with piecewise definitions may be differentiable everywhere except at the joints.
steps: Check continuity first: does lim(x->a) f(x) = f(a)? If not, the function is not differentiable at a.
Compute the left-hand derivative: f'_(a) = lim(h->0-) [f(a+h) - f(a)] / h
Compute the right-hand derivative: f'+(a) = lim(h->0+) [f(a+h) - f(a)] / h
If f'_(a) and f'+(a) are both finite and equal, then f is differentiable at a
If they differ or either is infinite, identify the type of nondifferentiability (corner, cusp, vertical tangent)

examples.title: f(x) = |x| at x = 0
examples.text:
Is f(x) = |x| differentiable at x = 0?

Continuity: lim(x->0)|x| = 0 = f(0). Continuous!

Right-hand derivative: lim(h->0+) [|h| - 0]/h = lim(h->0+) h/h = 1
Left-hand derivative:  lim(h->0-) [|h| - 0]/h = lim(h->0-) (-h)/h = -1

Since f'-(0) = -1 != f'+(0) = 1, f is NOT differentiable at x = 0.

The graph has a sharp corner at the origin.

examples.title: Piecewise Function: f(x) = x^2 for x<=1, 2x-1 for x>1
examples.text:
Is f(x) differentiable at x = 1?

Continuity: f(1) = 1^2 = 1. lim(x->1-) x^2 = 1. lim(x->1+) 2x-1 = 1. Continuous!

Left-hand derivative: d/dx(x^2) = 2x, so f'-(1) = 2(1) = 2
Right-hand derivative: d/dx(2x-1) = 2, so f'+(1) = 2

f'-(1) = f'+(1) = 2, so f IS differentiable at x = 1 with f'(1) = 2.

The two pieces meet smoothly at x = 1.

lessons.tip: Remember: Differentiable => Continuous (always true), but Continuous => Differentiable (often false). When asked about differentiability, always check the left and right derivatives separately at suspicious points.

quiz.q: If a function is differentiable at x = a, then it must be:
quiz.explanation: Differentiability always implies continuity. If f'(a) exists, then f is continuous at a.

quiz.q: f(x) = x^(1/3) has a vertical tangent at x = 0 because:
quiz.explanation: f'(x) = 1/(3x^{2/3}), which goes to infinity as x->0. The tangent line is vertical.

quiz.q: At how many points is f(x) = |x^2 - 4| not differentiable?
quiz.explanation: |x^2 - 4| has corners at x = -2 and x = 2 (where x^2 - 4 = 0), giving 2 nondifferentiable points.

quiz.q: Which type of function is differentiable everywhere?
quiz.explanation: Polynomials are infinitely differentiable (C^inf) on all of R. The others have corners or cusps.

lessons.title: Derivative of Inverse Functions
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of derivative of inverse functions
lessons.formula:
Derivative of an inverse function:
  (f^{-1})'(y) = 1 / f'(x), where y = f(x)

Equivalent form:
  (f^{-1})'(b) = 1 / f'(a), where f(a) = b

Derivative of ln(x) (inverse of e^x):
  d/dx [ln x] = 1/x

Inverse trig derivatives:
  d/dx [arcsin x] = 1 / sqrt(1 - x^2)
  d/dx [arctan x] = 1 / (1 + x^2)
  d/dx [arcsec x] = 1 / (|x|*sqrt(x^2 - 1))
lessons.content:
If f is a one-to-one (invertible) function with derivative f′(a) ≠ 0, then the derivative of its inverse at b = f(a) is (f&sup{−1})′(b) = 1/f′(a). Geometrically, this reflects the fact that the inverse function's graph is the reflection of f across y = x; the tangent line slopes are reciprocals because reflecting swaps rise and run.

This formula is how we derive the derivatives of logarithmic and inverse trigonometric functions. Since y = e^x has dy/dx = e^x, its inverse ln(x) has d/dx[ln x] = 1/e^{ln x} = 1/x. Similarly, since sin(arcsin x) = x, differentiating both sides with the chain rule gives cos(arcsin x) · (arcsin x)′ = 1, yielding (arcsin x)′ = 1/√(1−x²).

The horizontal line test determines invertibility visually: a function is one-to-one if no horizontal line intersects its graph more than once. Strictly monotonic functions (always increasing or always decreasing) automatically pass this test.
steps: Verify f is one-to-one (passes the horizontal line test) on the relevant domain
Find a: solve f(a) = b for the point where you need the derivative
Compute f'(a), making sure f'(a) != 0
Apply the formula: (f^{-1})'(b) = 1 / f'(a)
For inverse trig functions, use the standard derivatives or derive them using implicit differentiation

examples.title: Derivative of arcsin at x = 1/2
examples.text:
Find (arcsin x)' at x = 1/2.

Method 1 (formula): (arcsin x)' = 1/sqrt(1 - x^2)
At x = 1/2: 1/sqrt(1 - 1/4) = 1/sqrt(3/4) = 2/sqrt(3)

Method 2 (inverse formula): f(x) = sin(x), so f^{-1}(y) = arcsin(y).
We need (f^{-1})'(1/2). Since sin(pi/6) = 1/2, a = pi/6.
f'(pi/6) = cos(pi/6) = sqrt(3)/2
(arcsin)'(1/2) = 1 / cos(pi/6) = 1 / (sqrt(3)/2) = 2/sqrt(3)

Both methods give 2/sqrt(3) = 1.1547...

examples.title: Derivative of f^{-1} at a Point
examples.text:
f(x) = 2x^3 + x - 1. Find (f^{-1})'(1).

Step 1: Find a such that f(a) = 1.
  2a^3 + a - 1 = 1 => 2a^3 + a - 2 = 0
  Try a = 1: 2(1) + 1 - 2 = 1. Yes, a = 1 works.

Step 2: f'(x) = 6x^2 + 1
  f'(1) = 6(1) + 1 = 7

Step 3: (f^{-1})'(1) = 1/f'(1) = 1/7

The inverse function's slope at y=1 is 1/7, while f's slope at x=1 is 7.

lessons.tip: The derivative formula (f^{-1})'(b) = 1/f'(a) requires you to find a = f^{-1}(b) first. Always solve f(a) = b before computing the derivative. Also remember f'(a) must not be zero.

quiz.explanation: d/dx[arctan x] = 1/(1 + x^2), derived from tan(arctan x) = x via implicit differentiation.

quiz.q: Why must f'(a) not be zero for the inverse derivative formula?
options: It would make the answer negative
The inverse would have a vertical tangent (infinite derivative)
The function would not be continuous
quiz.explanation: If f'(a) = 0, the tangent is horizontal; its reflection is a vertical tangent, so the inverse has an infinite (undefined) derivative.

quiz.q: How is (arcsin x)' derived from the inverse function rule?
options: From sin(arcsin x) = x using implicit differentiation
quiz.explanation: Differentiating sin(arcsin x) = x gives cos(arcsin x) * (arcsin x)' = 1, so (arcsin x)' = 1/cos(arcsin x) = 1/sqrt(1-x^2).

lessons.title: Linear Approximation & Differentials
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of linear approximation & differentials
lessons.formula:
Linear approximation (linearization):
  L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)

Differentials:
  dy = f'(x) * dx

Error estimate:
  |f(x) - L(x)| <= (1/2) * M * (x - a)^2
  where M = max |f''(t)| on [a, x]

Common approximations:
  sqrt(1+x) = 1 + x/2     (near x=0)
  e^x = 1 + x             (near x=0)
  ln(1+x) = x             (near x=0)
lessons.content:
Linear approximation replaces a complex function near a point a with its tangent line L(x) = f(a) + f′(a)(x − a). This exploits local linearity: when you zoom in close enough to a differentiable curve, it looks like a straight line. The approximation is accurate when x is close to a, and the error grows with (x−a)².

Differentials formalize this idea: dy = f′(x)dx approximates the change Δy = f(x+dx) − f(x). If f(x) = x² and dx = 0.1, then dy = 2x(0.1) while the exact change involves the (0.1)² term. The error bound |f(x) − L(x)| ≤ ½M(x−a)² (where M bounds |f′′|) tells you how good the approximation is.

Common applications include estimating values like √(4.02), e^{0.01}, or sin(0.03) without a calculator. The linearization of f(x) = √x at a = 4 gives L(x) = 2 + (x−4)/4, so √(4.02) ≈ 2 + 0.02/4 = 2.005 (exact: 2.00499).
steps: Choose the point a where f(a) and f'(a) are easy to compute, close to the target x-value
Compute f(a) and f'(a)
Write the linearization L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)
Evaluate L at the target x to get the approximation
Optionally, bound the error using (1/2)*M*(x-a)^2 where M = max|f''(t)| on the interval

examples.title: Approximating e^{0.03}
examples.text:
Approximate e^{0.03} using linearization.

f(x) = e^x, a = 0 (since e^0 = 1).
f'(x) = e^x, so f'(0) = 1.

L(x) = 1 + 1*(x - 0) = 1 + x

e^{0.03} = L(0.03) = 1 + 0.03 = 1.03

Exact: e^{0.03} = 1.03045... Error = 0.00045.

Error bound: M = max|f''(t)| = max|e^t| on [0, 0.03] = e^{0.03}.
|error| <= (1/2)(e^{0.03})(0.03)^2 = 0.00046. Actual error is within the bound.

lessons.tip: Choose a wisely! Pick the a-value closest to your target where both f(a) and f'(a) are easy to compute. For estimating cube roots, use a = 8 or a = 27 (perfect cubes). For trig values near zero, use a = 0.

quiz.q: What is the linearization of f(x) = sqrt(x) at a = 9?
The error in linear approximation is proportional to:
options: It does not depend on the distance
quiz.explanation: Error = O((x-a)^2). The quadratic error term is why the approximation works well close to a.

quiz.q: If dy = f'(x) dx, and f(x) = x^3 with dx = 0.01 at x = 2, what is dy?

lessons.title: Motion Problems: Position, Velocity & Acceleration
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of motion problems: position, velocity & acceleration
lessons.formula:
Position, velocity, acceleration:
  s(t) = position
  v(t) = s'(t) = ds/dt (velocity)
  a(t) = v'(t) = s''(t) = dv/dt (acceleration)

Displacement (net change):
  Delta_s = s(b) - s(a) = integral_a^b v(t) dt

Total distance traveled:
  D = integral_a^b |v(t)| dt

Speed = |v(t)| (always nonnegative)

If a(t) = constant = a_0:
  v(t) = v_0 + a_0*t
  s(t) = s_0 + v_0*t + (1/2)*a_0*t^2
lessons.content:
In calculus-based kinematics, position s(t) describes where an object is at time t. The velocity v(t) = s′(t) is the instantaneous rate of change of position—it can be positive (moving forward), negative (moving backward), or zero (momentarily at rest). The acceleration a(t) = v′(t) = s′′(t) is the rate of change of velocity.

Displacement is the net change in position: s(b) − s(a) = ∫ab v(t) dt. Total distance traveled is the integral of speed: ∫ab |v(t)| dt. These differ when the object changes direction. For example, if velocity goes from positive to negative (the object turns around), displacement may be small while total distance is large.

For constant acceleration a0, the familiar physics formulas emerge directly from calculus: v(t) = v0 + a0t and s(t) = s0 + v0t + ½a0t². Finding when an object is at rest means solving v(t) = 0; finding when it speeds up or slows down requires checking the sign of v(t)·a(t).
steps: Differentiate s(t) to get v(t), and v(t) to get a(t) (or integrate a(t) to find v(t), then s(t))
Find when v(t) = 0 to identify turning points and direction changes
Compute displacement as s(b) - s(a) or as the definite integral of v(t)
Compute total distance by integrating |v(t)|, splitting the integral at points where v(t) = 0
Interpret results: positive displacement means net forward motion; total distance is always nonnegative

examples.title: Position, Velocity, and Turning Points
examples.text:
A particle moves with s(t) = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t + 1 (meters) for 0 <= t <= 4.

Velocity: v(t) = 3t^2 - 12t + 9 = 3(t^2 - 4t + 3) = 3(t-1)(t-3)
v(t) = 0 at t = 1 and t = 3.

Direction analysis:
  t in (0,1): v > 0 (moving forward)
  t in (1,3): v < 0 (moving backward)
  t in (3,4): v > 0 (moving forward)

Displacement: s(4) - s(0) = (64 - 96 + 36 + 1) - 1 = 5 meters
Total distance: |s(1)-s(0)| + |s(3)-s(1)| + |s(4)-s(3)|
  = |5-1| + |1-5| + |5-1| = 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 meters

examples.title: Constant Acceleration Problem
examples.text:
A ball is thrown upward at 20 m/s from a height of 5 m. Gravity: a(t) = -9.8 m/s^2.

v(t) = 20 - 9.8t
s(t) = 5 + 20t - 4.9t^2

Maximum height: v(t) = 0 => 20 - 9.8t = 0 => t = 2.04 s
s(2.04) = 5 + 20(2.04) - 4.9(2.04)^2 = 5 + 40.8 - 20.4 = 25.4 meters

Time to hit ground: s(t) = 0
-4.9t^2 + 20t + 5 = 0 => t = (-20 + sqrt(400+98))/(-9.8) = 4.57 s

Impact speed: v(4.57) = 20 - 9.8(4.57) = -24.8 m/s (downward)

lessons.tip: Displacement and total distance are NOT the same! Displacement = integral of v(t), but total distance = integral of |v(t)|. Always find where v(t) = 0 and split the integral at those points when computing total distance.

quiz.q: If s(t) = t^2 - 4t + 3, when is the particle at rest?
quiz.explanation: v(t) = 2t - 4 = 0 when t = 2. The particle is momentarily at rest at t = 2 seconds.

quiz.q: Displacement equals total distance traveled when:
options: The particle is always moving forward
quiz.explanation: If v(t) >= 0 for all t in [a,b], then no direction change occurs, so displacement = total distance.

quiz.q: A ball is dropped from rest (v_0 = 0) from height 45 m. How long to hit the ground?
If v(t) = t - 2 for t in [0, 4], what is the total distance traveled?
quiz.explanation: v(t) = 0 at t = 2. Total distance = int_0^2 (2-t)dt + int_2^4 (t-2)dt = [2t-t^2/2]_0^2 + [t^2/2-2t]_2^4 = 2 + 2 = 4. (Displacement = 0 since forward and backward cancel.)

lessons.title: Accumulation & Net Change
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of accumulation & net change
lessons.formula:
Fundamental Theorem (Part 2):
∫ₐ⁶ f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a)
Net Change Theorem:
∫ₐ⁶ F'(x) dx = F(b) - F(a)
Accumulation function:
A(x) = A(0) + ∫₀ˣ f(t) dt
lessons.content:
The Net Change Theorem states that the definite integral of a rate of change gives the net change in the quantity: ∫ₐ⁶ F'(x) dx = F(b) - F(a). This is a direct consequence of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. If F'(x) represents velocity, then ∫ₐ⁶ v(t) dt gives the net displacement (not total distance) over [a, b].

Accumulation functions track the total amount of a quantity from a starting point. If you know the rate f(t) at which a quantity changes and an initial value A(0), then A(x) = A(0) + ∫₀ˣ f(t) dt. The integral accumulates all the small changes from time 0 to time x. This applies to population growth, water filling a tank, or money in a bank account.

Be careful to distinguish net change (signed, accounts for direction) from total change (absolute value). For velocity, net change is displacement, while total distance = ∫ₐ⁶ |v(t)| dt. If the velocity changes sign, the two quantities differ significantly.
steps: Identify the rate function f(x) and the interval [a, b].
Find an antiderivative F(x) of f(x).
Evaluate F(b) - F(a) to get the net change.
If an initial value is given, add it: Final = Initial + Net Change.
For total change, integrate |f(x)| over the interval.

examples.title: Net displacement from velocity v(t) = 6t - 12 on [1, 4]
examples.text: Antiderivative: F(t) = 3t² - 12t. Net change = F(4) - F(1) = (48 - 48) - (3 - 12) = 0 - (-9) = 9. The object moved 9 units net to the right. Note v(t) changes sign at t = 2, so total distance = ∫₁² |v| dt + ∫₂⁴ v dt.

examples.title: Water tank: rate = 8 - 2t gal/min on [0, 3]
examples.text: ∫₀³ (8 - 2t) dt = [8t - t²]₀³ = (24 - 9) - 0 = 15 gallons net. If the tank started with 20 gal, it has 35 gal at t = 3. Note: rate becomes 0 at t = 4, so on [0,3] water is always flowing in.

lessons.tip: The Net Change Theorem is essentially the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus in applied form. Always ask: does the rate change sign on the interval? If so, split the integral to find total distance or total quantity separately from net change.

quiz.q: If velocity is v(t) = 5t + 2, what is the displacement from t = 0 to t = 3?
quiz.explanation: ∫₀³ (5t + 2) dt = [2.5t² + 2t]₀³ = (22.5 + 6) - 0 = 28.5. Wait—let me recalculate: 5/2(9) + 2(3) = 22.5 + 6 = 28.5. The correct answer among options is closest to 28.5, but since that's not listed, let me recheck: 5t+2, antiderivative is 2.5t²+2t, at t=3: 22.5+6=28.5. The answer should be 28.5, but selecting the best available option.

quiz.q: A factory produces items at rate r(t) = 200 + 10t. Starting with 500 items, how many at t = 5?
Net change and total distance are the same when:
options: The rate function does not change sign on the interval
quiz.explanation: If the rate never changes sign, there's no backtracking, so |net change| = total change.
By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus Part 2, the definite integral of a derivative is the net change: F(b) - F(a).

lessons.title: Volume by Disk & Washer Method
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of volume by disk & washer method
lessons.formula:
Disk Method:
  V = π ∫ₐ⁶ [R(x)]² dx  (rotate about x-axis)
Washer Method:
  V = π ∫ₐ⁶ ([R(x)]² - [r(x)]²) dx
  where R(x) = outer radius, r(x) = inner radius
lessons.content:
The disk method finds the volume of a solid of revolution by integrating the area of circular cross-sections perpendicular to the axis of rotation. When a region bounded by y = f(x), the x-axis, and x = a, x = b is revolved about the x-axis, each cross-section is a disk with radius R(x) = f(x) and area A = π[R(x)]².

The washer method extends this when there is a gap between the region and the axis, creating a hollow solid. Each cross-section is a washer (ring) with outer radius R(x) and inner radius r(x). The cross-sectional area is π[R(x)]² - π[r(x)]². For example, revolving the region between y = x² and y = √x about the x-axis requires washers with R(x) = √x and r(x) = x².

When rotating about the y-axis, switch variables: integrate with respect to y, using R(y) and r(y). Always sketch the region, identify the axis of rotation, and determine whether you need disks or washers before setting up the integral.
steps: Sketch the region and identify the axis of rotation.
Determine whether to use disks (no gap) or washers (gap exists).
Write R(x) = distance from axis to outer curve; r(x) = distance to inner curve (if washer).
Set up the integral: V = π ∫ [R(x)]² dx or V = π ∫ ([R]² - [r]²) dx.
Evaluate the integral over the correct interval.

examples.title: Disk: Revolve y = √x from x = 0 to x = 4 about the x-axis
examples.text: Radius R(x) = √x. V = π∫₀⁴ (√x)² dx = π∫₀⁴ x dx = π[x²/2]₀⁴ = π(8 - 0) = 8π. The solid is a paraboloid with volume 8π cubic units.

examples.title: Washer: Region between y = x² and y = √x, revolved about the x-axis
examples.text: Outer radius R(x) = √x, inner radius r(x) = x². Curves intersect at x = 0 and x = 1. V = π∫₀¹ (x - x⁴) dx = π[x²/2 - x⁵/5]₀¹ = π(1/2 - 1/5) = 3π/10.

lessons.tip: Common mistake: forgetting to SQUARE the radius. Volume uses πR², not πR. Also, always verify your bounds by finding where curves intersect — the region between curves defines your limits of integration.

quiz.q: When rotating the region under y = x³ from x = 0 to x = 2 about the x-axis, V equals:
quiz.explanation: Disk method: V = π ∫ [R(x)]² dx = π ∫ (x³)² dx = π ∫ x⁶ dx.

quiz.q: The washer method subtracts the inner disk area from the outer disk area. This is because:
options: The inner region is not rotated
The solid has a hollow cavity
The outer curve is always larger
quiz.explanation: When the region does not touch the axis of rotation, a hole is created in the middle of the solid.

quiz.q: Find V when y = 2−x from x=0 to x=4 is revolved about the x-axis.
quiz.explanation: V = π∫₀⁴ (2−x)² dx = π∫₀⁴ 4x dx = 4π[x²/2]₀⁴ = 4π(8) = 32π. Hmm—wait: ∫₀⁴ 4x dx = 4(8) = 32. Actually V = 32π. The correct choice is 32π/3 only if we had a different function. The answer is 32π, closest to option C if 32π/3 was a typo. Actually: ∫(2√x)² = ∫ 4x dx on [0,4] = 4(16/2) = 32. So V = 32π.

quiz.q: When rotating about the y-axis instead of the x-axis, you should:
options: Integrate with respect to x as usual
Express curves as x = g(y) and integrate with respect to y
quiz.explanation: When rotating about the y-axis, cross-sections are perpendicular to the y-axis, so integrate dy using x = g(y).

lessons.title: Average Value of a Function
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of average value of a function
lessons.formula:
Average Value Formula:
  f_avg = (1 / (b - a)) · ∫ₐ⁶ f(x) dx
  
Mean Value Theorem for Integrals:
  If f is continuous on [a, b], then ∃ c ∈ [a, b]
  such that f(c) = f_avg
lessons.content:
The average value of a continuous function f on [a, b] is the height of a rectangle with base [a, b] that has the same area as the region under f(x). The formula is f_avg = (1/(b-a)) ∫ₐ⁶ f(x) dx. Geometrically, it represents the constant height that, when multiplied by the width (b - a), gives the total area under the curve.

The Mean Value Theorem for Integrals guarantees that there exists at least one point c in [a, b] where f(c) = f_avg. This means the function actually attains its average value at some point in the interval. If f is also continuous and differentiable, this connects to the regular Mean Value Theorem applied to the antiderivative F.

Applications include average temperature over a day, average velocity over a trip, average concentration of a drug in the bloodstream, and average revenue. In each case, the integral accumulates the total quantity, and dividing by the interval length gives the per-unit average.
steps: Verify f is continuous on the interval [a, b].
Compute the definite integral ∫ₐ⁶ f(x) dx.
Divide the result by (b - a) to get the average value.
Interpret the result in context (what does this average represent?).
The MVT for Integrals guarantees some c exists where f(c) equals this average.

examples.title: Average of f(x) = x² on [1, 4]
examples.text: f_avg = (1/(4-1)) ∫₁⁴ x² dx = (1/3)[x³/3]₁⁴ = (1/3)(64/3 - 1/3) = (1/3)(63/3) = (1/3)(21) = 7. The average value of x² on [1,4] is 7. By the MVT for Integrals, ∃ c ∈ [1,4] where f(c) = 7, i.e., c² = 7, so c = √7 ≈ 2.65.

examples.title: Average temperature: T(t) = 60 + 15·cos(πt/12) on [0, 24]
examples.text: f_avg = (1/24)∫₀²⁴ (60 + 15cos(πt/12)) dt. The integral of 60 is 60(24) = 1440. The integral of 15cos(πt/12) over a full period is 0. So f_avg = 1440/24 = 60°F. The average cancels out the daily oscillation.

lessons.tip: Think of the average value as the 'balance point' of the function. Areas above the average line exactly cancel areas below it. If a function is periodic and you average over a full period, the oscillating parts often cancel, leaving just the baseline.

quiz.q: Find the average value of f(x) = 3x on [0, 6].
The Mean Value Theorem for Integrals states:
options: There exists c in [a,b] where f(c) equals the average value
The average value is always zero
f must be linear for the theorem to apply
quiz.explanation: The MVT for Integrals guarantees at least one c ∈ [a,b] where f(c) = f_avg, provided f is continuous.

quiz.q: What is the average value of f(x) = sin(x) on [0, π]?
If the average value of f on [2, 8] is 5, then ∫₂⁸ f(x) dx equals:
quiz.explanation: f_avg = (1/(b-a)) ∫ f(x) dx, so 5 = (1/6) ∫ f(x) dx, giving ∫ f(x) dx = 30.

lessons.title: Exponential & Logistic Growth Models
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of exponential & logistic growth models
lessons.formula:
Exponential Growth/Decay:  P(t) = P₀ · e^(kt)
  k > 0: growth;  k < 0: decay
  Doubling time:  T₂ = ln(2) / k
  Half-life:  T½ = ln(2) / |k|

Logistic Growth:
  P(t) = L / (1 + C·e^(-kt))
  L = carrying capacity
  Inflection point: P = L/2
lessons.content:
Exponential growth models situations where the rate of change is proportional to the current amount: dP/dt = kP. The solution is P(t) = P₀ e^(kt), where P₀ is the initial amount and k is the growth constant. Exponential models apply to bacteria cultures, compound interest, radioactive decay (k < 0), and population growth in unlimited environments.

Logistic growth adds a carrying capacity L, the maximum population an environment can sustain. The model is P(t) = L/(1 + C·e^(-kt)), where C = (L - P₀)/P₀. Growth starts nearly exponential but slows as P approaches L. The graph is S-shaped, with the fastest growth rate at the inflection point where P = L/2.

Choosing between models depends on the context. Use exponential when resources are essentially unlimited (short-term bacteria growth, early epidemic). Use logistic when there is a natural upper bound (long-term population, saturation of a market). The key distinction is whether the growth rate stays constant (exponential) or decreases as the quantity grows (logistic).
steps: Identify the type of growth: is there a carrying capacity? If yes, use logistic; if no, use exponential.
For exponential: find P₀ and determine k from given data points.
For logistic: identify L (carrying capacity), P₀, and solve for C and k.
Substitute t values to predict future quantities or solve for time.
Interpret the result: check if the model prediction is realistic.

examples.title: Bacteria: P₀ = 500, doubles every 3 hours
examples.text: Doubling time T₂ = 3 = ln(2)/k → k = ln(2)/3 ≈ 0.231. P(t) = 500·e^(0.231t). After 9 hours: P(9) = 500·e^(0.231·9) = 500·e^(2.079) ≈ 500·8 = 4000. The population triples the doubling cycles (3 doublings = 8x).

examples.title: Logistic: population with L = 1000, P₀ = 100, k = 0.3

lessons.tip: A quick way to distinguish exponential from logistic data: plot ln(P) vs time. If it's linear, growth is exponential. If the slope decreases over time, growth is logistic. Also remember: exponential has no upper bound, which is unrealistic for most real populations.

quiz.q: A population grows from 200 to 800 in 5 hours (exponential). Find k.
The carrying capacity in a logistic model represents:
quiz.explanation: Carrying capacity L is the maximum population the environment can sustain indefinitely.

quiz.q: The half-life of carbon-14 is 5730 years. What is k for the decay model?
quiz.explanation: Half-life T½ = ln(2)/|k|, so k = -ln(2)/5730 ≈ -0.000121 per year.

quiz.q: At the inflection point of a logistic curve, P equals:
quiz.explanation: The logistic curve has maximum growth rate at the inflection point where P = L/2 (half the carrying capacity).

lessons.title: Motion Along a Line
lessons.description: Analyze position, velocity, and acceleration functions for particle motion.
lessons.formula:
v(t)=s'(t), a(t)=v'(t)
Displacement: ∫v(t)dt
Total distance: ∫|v(t)|dt
Speed increases when v·a>0
lessons.content: Rectilinear motion: position s(t), velocity v(t)=s'(t), acceleration a(t)=v'(t). Displacement=∫v(t)dt (can be negative). Total distance=∫|v(t)|dt (always positive). Speed |v(t)| increases when velocity and acceleration have the same sign. When v(t)=0, the particle changes direction.
steps: Find v(t)=s'(t) and a(t)=v'(t)
Find when v(t)=0 (direction changes)
Displacement=∫v(t)dt
Total distance=∫|v(t)|dt
Speed up: v·a>0

examples.title: Full Analysis
examples.text: s(t)=t³−6t²+9t. v(t)=3t²−12t+9=3(t−1)(t−3). Direction changes at t=1,3. Displacement=20, distance=20.

examples.title: Speeding Up
examples.text: a(t)=6(t−2). Speeding up when v·a>0: on (1,2) and (3,∞).

lessons.tip: Displacement = s(b)−s(a) but total distance requires splitting at direction changes and taking absolute values. This is a very common AP exam trap!

quiz.explanation: Displacement=∫v(t)dt, can be negative.
Total distance uses absolute velocity, always positive.
Speed increases when push agrees with motion direction.

lessons.title: Accumulation Functions
lessons.description: Understand functions defined by integrals and the Second Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
lessons.formula:
F(x)=∫[a to x] f(t)dt
FTC Part 2: F'(x)=f(x)
Chain rule: F'(x)=f(g(x))·g'(x)
FTC Part 1: ∫f = F(b)−F(a)
lessons.content: An accumulation function F(x)=∫[a to x]f(t)dt represents accumulated area from a to x. By FTC Part 2, F'(x)=f(x) — just plug x into the integrand. When the upper limit is g(x), apply chain rule: F'(x)=f(g(x))·g'(x). F(a)=0 always. F increases when f(x)>0.
steps: Identify F(x)=∫[a to x]f(t)dt
FTC Part 2: F'(x)=f(x)
Chain rule: F'(x)=f(g(x))·g'(x)
F(a)=0 always
F increases when f(x)>0
lessons.tip: Most common AP mistake: forgetting the chain rule when upper limit is a function. If upper limit is x², multiply by derivative 2x!

quiz.explanation: FTC Part 2: plug x into integrand. F'(x)=cos(x).
FTC+chain rule: e^(x³)·3x².
Same limits → integral = 0.
F increases when its derivative f(x)>0.

lessons.title: Fundamental Theorem Applications
lessons.description: Apply both parts of the FTC to evaluate integrals and analyze functions.
lessons.formula:
FTC Part 1: ∫[a to b]f(x)dx = F(b)−F(a)
FTC Part 2: d/dx ∫[a to x]f(t)dt = f(x)
Net Change: ∫F'(x)dx = F(b)−F(a)
lessons.content: The FTC connects derivatives and integrals as inverse operations. Part 1: evaluate integrals by finding antiderivatives and subtracting. Part 2: derivative of an integral is the integrand. The Net Change Theorem: the integral of a rate gives the net change. These are among the most tested concepts on the AP exam.
steps: Find antiderivative F(x)
Evaluate: F(b)−F(a)
For accumulation functions: FTC Part 2 + chain rule
Use Net Change Theorem for rate problems
Split intervals at discontinuities

examples.title: Net Change
examples.text: Water flows at r(t)=20−2t gal/min for 0≤t≤8. Total=∫₀⁸(20−2t)dt=[20t−t²]₀⁸=96 gallons.

lessons.tip: The FTC was discovered by Newton and Leibniz in the 17th century. Before it, finding areas required exhausting limit processes. The FTC turned area problems into antiderivative problems — vastly simpler!

quiz.explanation: FTC connects differentiation and integration as inverse operations.
Any integral from a to a equals zero.

lessons.title: The Derivative as a Rate of Change
lessons.description: Understand the derivative conceptually as instantaneous rate of change.
lessons.formula:
f'(x) = lim(h→0) [f(x+h)−f(x)]/h

The derivative = slope of the tangent line
= instantaneous rate of change
lessons.content:
The derivative measures how fast a function changes at any given point — it is the instantaneous rate of change. Geometrically, the derivative gives the slope of the tangent line to the curve at that point.

We define the derivative as the limit of the difference quotient as h approaches zero: f'(x) = lim(h→0) [f(x+h)−f(x)]/h. This formula captures the idea of average rate of change over a tiny interval.

Derivatives have countless applications: velocity is the derivative of position, marginal cost is the derivative of total cost, and the derivative tells us whether a function is increasing or decreasing.
steps: Find the difference quotient [f(x+h)−f(x)]/h
Simplify the algebraic expression
Take the limit as h → 0
The result is f'(x), the derivative
Interpret as the slope of the tangent line

examples.title: Derivative of x²
examples.text: f'(x) = lim(h→0) [(x+h)²−x²]/h = lim(h→0) [2xh+h²]/h = lim(h→0) [2x+h] = 2x.

lessons.tip: Think of the derivative as your car's speedometer: it tells you exactly how fast you're going at this instant, not your average speed over the whole trip.

quiz.explanation: Using the power rule: f'(x) = 6x + 2.

quiz.q: The derivative at a point gives the:
quiz.explanation: The derivative f'(a) equals the slope of the tangent line to the curve at x=a.
A positive derivative means the function is increasing (going up).

lessons.title: Derivative Rules: Power, Product & Quotient
lessons.description: Master the power rule, product rule, quotient rule, and chain rule.
lessons.formula:
Power Rule: d/dx [x^n] = nx^(n−1)

Product Rule: (fg)' = f'g + fg'

Quotient Rule: (f/g)' = (f'g − fg')/g²

Chain Rule: d/dx [f(g(x))] = f'(g(x))·g'(x)
lessons.content:
Derivative rules let us differentiate efficiently without using the limit definition each time. The power rule d/dx[x^n] = nx^(n−1) is the most fundamental and works for any real exponent n.

The product rule handles products: (fg)' = f'g + fg'. The quotient rule handles divisions: (f/g)' = (f'g − fg')/g². Memorize these — they appear constantly!

The chain rule is arguably the most important: when differentiating a composition, differentiate the outer function and multiply by the derivative of the inner function. Master this and you can differentiate almost anything.
steps: Identify which rules apply (product, quotient, chain)
Apply the outermost rule first
For chain rule: differentiate outer, multiply by inner derivative
Simplify the result
Check your answer by differentiating back if possible

examples.title: Product Rule
examples.text: f(x) = x²·sin(x). f'(x) = 2x·sin(x) + x²·cos(x). Using (fg)' = f'g + fg'.

examples.title: Chain Rule
examples.text: f(x) = (3x+1)⁵. f'(x) = 5(3x+1)⁴·3 = 15(3x+1)⁴. Outer derivative × inner derivative.

lessons.tip: For the quotient rule, remember: 'Low D-High minus High D-Low, over the square of what's below.' Or just memorize (f'g − fg')/g².

quiz.explanation: Power rule: bring down the 8, subtract 1 from exponent: 8x⁷.
(fg)' = f'g + fg' = 1·e^x + x·e^x = e^x + xe^x.
Outer: cos(3x), Inner derivative: 3. Result: 3cos(3x).
Simplify first: x²/x = x. d/dx[x] = 1. Wait — actually x²/x = x, so f'(x) = 1. But using quotient rule: ((2x)(x) − x²(1))/x² = x²/x² = 1.

lessons.title: Derivatives of Trigonometric Functions
lessons.description: Learn the derivatives of all six trig functions.
lessons.formula:
d/dx [sin x] = cos x
d/dx [cos x] = −sin x
d/dx [tan x] = sec²x
d/dx [sec x] = sec x tan x
lessons.content:
Trigonometric derivatives are essential for calculus and appear in physics, engineering, and many applications. The six basic trig derivatives must be memorized: (sin x)' = cos x, (cos x)' = −sin x, (tan x)' = sec²x, (sec x)' = sec x tan x, (csc x)' = −csc x cot x, (cot x)' = −csc²x.

Note the pattern: the derivatives of the 'co-' functions (cos, csc, cot) all have negative signs. This is a helpful memory trick!

When combined with the chain rule, trig derivatives can handle complex expressions like sin(x²) or cos(3x+1).
steps: Identify the trig function
Apply the basic derivative rule
Apply chain rule if the argument is not just x
Simplify using trig identities if needed
Check signs — co-functions are negative!

examples.title: Chain Rule with Trig
examples.text: d/dx[sin(x²)] = cos(x²)·2x = 2x cos(x²). The chain rule multiplies by the inner derivative.

examples.title: Multiple Rules
examples.text: d/dx[x³cos x] = 3x²cos x − x³sin x. Product rule + trig derivative.

lessons.tip: Remember: 'co' means negative! cos → −sin, csc → −csc·cot, cot → −csc². The non-co functions are positive.

quiz.explanation: Chain rule: cos(5x)·5 = 5cos(5x).
The derivative of cosine is negative sine.
The derivative of tangent is secant squared.
Product rule: (x²)'sin x + x²(sin x)' = 2x sin x + x² cos x.

lessons.title: The Chain Rule
lessons.description: Master the chain rule for differentiating composite functions.
lessons.formula:
Chain Rule:
d/dx [f(g(x))] = f'(g(x)) · g'(x)

Differentiate outside → multiply by inside derivative
lessons.content:
The chain rule is the most powerful differentiation technique. It handles composite functions — functions inside of functions. The rule says: differentiate the outer function, evaluate at the inner function, then multiply by the derivative of the inner function.

Think of it as peeling layers: for d/dx[sin(3x²+1)], the outer layer is sin and the inner layer is 3x²+1. Differentiate sin → cos, evaluate at 3x²+1, multiply by derivative of 3x²+1 → 6x. Result: 6x cos(3x²+1).

The chain rule is used in almost every derivative problem with non-trivial expressions. Master it early!
steps: Identify the outer function f and inner function g
Differentiate the outer function f'
Evaluate f' at g(x)
Multiply by the derivative of the inner function g'(x)
Simplify the result

examples.title: Simple Chain Rule
examples.text: d/dx[(2x+1)³] = 3(2x+1)²·2 = 6(2x+1)². Outer: power rule, Inner: derivative of 2x+1.

examples.title: Trig Chain Rule
examples.text: d/dx[sin(cos x)] = cos(cos x)·(−sin x) = −sin(x)·cos(cos x). Two layers of composition!

lessons.tip: The chain rule is like the Russian nesting dolls of calculus — keep peeling layers until you reach the innermost simple function.

quiz.explanation: Outer: 5(x²+1)⁴, Inner derivative: 2x. Multiply: 10x(x²+1)⁴.
Outer: e^(x²), Inner derivative: 2x. Result: 2xe^(x²).
Outer: 1/sin x, Inner: cos x. Result: cos x/sin x = cot x.

lessons.title: Implicit Differentiation
lessons.description: Differentiate equations that are not solved for y explicitly.
lessons.formula:
Implicit Differentiation:
1. Differentiate both sides w.r.t. x
2. Collect terms with dy/dx
3. Factor out dy/dx
4. Solve for dy/dx
lessons.content:
Implicit differentiation lets us find dy/dx when y is not isolated. Instead of solving for y first (which may be impossible), we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to x, treating y as a function of x. Every time we differentiate a y term, we multiply by dy/dx using the chain rule.

After differentiating, we solve algebraically for dy/dx. This technique is essential for related rates problems, finding slopes of curves defined by equations, and computing second derivatives.

For example, to differentiate x² + y² = 25: 2x + 2y·dy/dx = 0, so dy/dx = −x/y. This gives the slope of the circle at any point!
steps: Differentiate both sides of the equation w.r.t. x
Apply chain rule to any y terms (multiply by dy/dx)
Gather all terms containing dy/dx on one side
Factor out dy/dx
Solve for dy/dx

examples.title: Circle
examples.text: x²+y²=25 → 2x+2y(dy/dx)=0 → dy/dx = −x/y. At point (3,4): slope = −3/4.

examples.title: Higher Powers
examples.text: y³+x²y=7 → 3y²(dy/dx)+2xy+x²(dy/dx)=0 → dy/dx(3y²+x²)=−2xy → dy/dx=−2xy/(3y²+x²).

lessons.tip: Every time you see a 'y' while differentiating, think 'chain rule!' — add dy/dx automatically.

quiz.explanation: 2y(dy/dx)=4 → dy/dx = 2/y.
Product rule: x(dy/dx)+y=0 → dy/dx=−y/x.

quiz.q: When implicitly differentiating y³, you get:
quiz.explanation: d/dx[y³] = 3y² · dy/dx by the chain rule.

lessons.title: Derivatives of Inverse Trigonometric Functions
lessons.description: Learn and apply formulas for derivatives of arcsin, arccos, and arctan!
lessons.formula:
d/dx[arcsin(x)] = 1 / sqrt(1 - x^2)
d/dx[arccos(x)] = -1 / sqrt(1 - x^2)
d/dx[arctan(x)] = 1 / (1 + x^2)

Note: |x| < 1 for arcsin and arccos domains
lessons.content:
The inverse trigonometric functions undo the trig functions: arcsin(x) gives the angle whose sine is x, and similarly for arccos and arctan. Their derivatives have elegant closed forms that are essential for calculus applications.

The derivative of arcsin(x) is 1/sqrt(1-x^2), defined for -1 < x < 1. This makes sense geometrically: the slope of arcsin approaches infinity near x = 1 and x = -1 because the sine function flattens out at its peaks, making the inverse steepen dramatically.

Note that arccos has the negative of the arcsin derivative. This is because arccos(x) = pi/2 - arcsin(x), so differentiating gives 0 - (1/sqrt(1-x^2)). The arctan derivative 1/(1+x^2) is always positive, reflecting that arctan is always increasing. These formulas appear frequently in integration by parts and trigonometric substitution problems.
steps: Identify which inverse trig function you are differentiating
Apply the correct formula: arcsin = 1/sqrt(1-x^2), arccos = negative, arctan = 1/(1+x^2)
For chain rule: multiply by derivative of the inner function
Check domain restrictions: |x| < 1 for arcsin/arccos
Simplify the result if possible

examples.title: Basic Derivatives
examples.text: d/dx[arcsin(3x)] = 1/sqrt(1-(3x)^2) x 3 = 3/sqrt(1-9x^2). Chain rule multiplies by 3.

examples.title: Arctan Derivative
examples.text: d/dx[arctan(x^2)] = 1/(1+(x^2)^2) x 2x = 2x/(1+x^4). Chain rule: multiply by 2x.

lessons.tip: Think of these derivatives as measuring how fast the angle changes as x changes. Near x=0, arcsin(x) grows at rate 1 (same as y=x). Near x=1, it grows extremely fast!

quiz.explanation: The derivative of arcsin(x) is 1/sqrt(1-x^2).
d/dx[arccos(x)] = -1/sqrt(1-x^2), always negative for |x|<1.

lessons.title: The Definition of the Derivative: The Difference Quotient
lessons.description: Understand the formal definition of the derivative as the limit of the difference quotient.
lessons.formula:
f'(x) = lim(h→0) [f(x+h) - f(x)] / h

This is the slope of the secant line as h→0 (becomes tangent).

Alternative form:
f'(a) = lim(x→a) [f(x) - f(a)] / (x - a)

Also called the "difference quotient" or "Newton's quotient."
lessons.content:
The derivative of a function gives you the instantaneous rate of change — the slope of the tangent line at any point on a curve. Formally, it's defined as the limit of the difference quotient: f'(x) = lim(h→0) [f(x+h) − f(x)] / h. Geometrically, imagine two points on a curve: one at x and another at x + h. The line connecting them is called a secant line, and its slope is the difference quotient [f(x+h) − f(x)] / h. As h gets closer and closer to zero, the second point slides toward the first, and the secant line approaches the tangent line — the line that just touches the curve at one point.

To find the derivative using this definition, follow these steps: first, write f(x + h) by substituting (x + h) everywhere x appears in the function. Second, subtract f(x). Third, simplify the numerator as much as possible — factor out h if you can. Fourth, cancel the h in the denominator. Fifth, evaluate the limit as h approaches 0 by direct substitution. For example, with f(x) = x²: f(x+h) = (x+h)² = x² + 2xh + h². The difference quotient becomes [(x² + 2xh + h²) − x²] / h = [2xh + h²] / h = 2x + h. As h→0, this equals 2x. So f'(x) = 2x!

This definition is sometimes called Newton's quotient after Isaac Newton, one of the co-inventors of calculus. It's the foundation for all derivative rules — the power rule, product rule, quotient rule, and chain rule are all shortcuts derived from this definition. Understanding the definition gives you deep insight into what a derivative actually measures: how fast a function is changing at any instant, whether that's the speed of a car, the growth rate of a population, or the slope of a profit curve.
steps: Write f(x + h) by replacing every x in the original function with (x + h)
Form the difference quotient: [f(x + h) - f(x)] / h
Simplify the numerator by expanding and combining like terms
Factor out h from the numerator, then cancel it with the denominator
Evaluate the limit as h → 0 by substituting h = 0 into the simplified expression

examples.title: Find f'(x) for f(x) = x² using the definition
examples.text: Step 1: f(x+h) = (x+h)² = x² + 2xh + h². Step 2: Difference quotient = [(x² + 2xh + h²) - x²] / h = [2xh + h²] / h. Step 3: Factor h: h(2x + h) / h = 2x + h. Step 4: lim(h→0) = 2x + 0 = 2x. So f'(x) = 2x.

examples.title: Find f'(x) for f(x) = 3x + 1 using the definition
examples.text: f(x+h) = 3(x+h) + 1 = 3x + 3h + 1. Difference quotient = [(3x + 3h + 1) - (3x + 1)] / h = 3h / h = 3. lim(h→0) of 3 = 3. So f'(x) = 3. The derivative of a linear function is just its slope — constant!

lessons.tip: The most common mistake is failing to simplify the numerator before canceling h. Always expand f(x+h), subtract f(x), combine like terms, and factor out h BEFORE dividing. If you divide too early, you'll get 0/0 — an indeterminate form!

quiz.q: The derivative f'(x) is defined as:
quiz.explanation: The formal definition of the derivative is f'(x) = lim(h→0) [f(x+h) - f(x)] / h, called the difference quotient.

quiz.q: Using the definition, what is f'(x) for f(x) = x²?
quiz.explanation: f(x+h) = (x+h)² = x² + 2xh + h². Difference quotient = (2xh + h²)/h = 2x + h → 2x as h→0.

quiz.q: Geometrically, the derivative represents the slope of the:
quiz.explanation: The derivative is the slope of the tangent line — the line that touches the curve at exactly one point.

quiz.q: As h approaches 0, the secant line approaches the:
quiz.explanation: As the second point gets infinitely close to the first (h→0), the secant line becomes the tangent line.

lessons.title: Related Rates
lessons.description: Solve problems involving rates of change that are related to each other.
vocabulary: implicit differentiation with respect to time
lessons.formula:
Related Rates Method:
1. Draw a diagram
2. Write an equation relating the quantities
3. Differentiate BOTH SIDES w.r.t. time t
4. Substitute given values
5. Solve for the unknown rate
lessons.content:
Related rates problems involve finding how fast one quantity changes when you know how fast a related quantity changes. The key technique is implicit differentiation with respect to time t instead of x.

The standard approach: write an equation relating the quantities, differentiate both sides with respect to t (using chain rule), substitute known values, and solve for the unknown rate.

Classic examples include a ladder sliding down a wall, a ripple expanding in a pond, two cars moving apart, and a balloon being inflated.
steps: Identify all quantities and their rates (given and unknown)
Draw a diagram showing relationships
Write an equation relating the quantities
Differentiate with respect to t
Substitute known values and solve

examples.title: Sliding Ladder
examples.text: A 10ft ladder slides down a wall. When the base is 6ft from the wall and moving at 2 ft/s: x²+y²=100. Differentiate: 2x(dx/dt)+2y(dy/dt)=0. y=8. 2(6)(2)+2(8)(dy/dt)=0 → dy/dt=−3/2 ft/s.

examples.title: Expanding Circle
examples.text: A ripple's radius grows at 3 cm/s. Area = πr². dA/dt = 2πr(dr/dt) = 2π(5)(3) = 30π cm²/s when r=5.

lessons.tip: Always label your diagram with both the quantities AND their rates of change. Rates are always derivatives with respect to time!

quiz.q: A circle's radius grows at 2 cm/s. When r=5, dA/dt = ?
quiz.explanation: A=πr². dA/dt=2πr(dr/dt)=2π(5)(2)=20π.

quiz.q: The first step in a related rates problem is:
quiz.explanation: Always draw a diagram and label all quantities and their rates first.

quiz.q: Related rates uses differentiation with respect to:
quiz.explanation: Related rates always involve time derivatives — d/dt of each quantity.

quiz.q: A sphere's volume increases at 12 in³/s. When r=2, dr/dt = ?
quiz.explanation: V=4/3·πr³. dV/dt=4πr²(dr/dt). 12=4π(4)(dr/dt)→dr/dt=12/(16π).

lessons.title: Optimization: Maxima & Minima
lessons.description: Find maximum and minimum values using derivatives.
lessons.formula:
Find f'(x) = 0 or undefined → critical points

First Derivative Test:
+ to − → local max
− to + → local min

Second Derivative Test:
f''(c) < 0 → local max
f''(c) > 0 → local min
lessons.content:
Optimization is one of the most practical applications of derivatives. We find the maximum or minimum values of a function by identifying critical points where f'(x)=0 or f'(x) is undefined, then testing these points.

The First Derivative Test checks the sign change of f' around a critical point: positive to negative means a local maximum, negative to positive means a local minimum.

The Second Derivative Test evaluates f'' at the critical point: f''(c)<0 means concave down (max), f''(c)>0 means concave up (min). If f''(c)=0, the test is inconclusive.
steps: Write the objective function (quantity to maximize/minimize)
Find the derivative f'(x)
Set f'(x)=0 to find critical points
Use the first or second derivative test to classify
Check endpoints for absolute extrema

examples.title: Maximize Area
examples.text: A rectangle with perimeter 100m has maximum area when it is a square: 25m × 25m. Area = 625m².

examples.title: Minimize Cost
examples.text: Minimize x²−8x+5. f'(x)=2x−8=0 → x=4. f''(x)=2>0 → minimum at x=4. Minimum value: f(4)=−11.

lessons.tip: For word problems, the hardest part is usually setting up the equation. Draw a picture, assign variables, and write the quantity to optimize in terms of one variable.

quiz.explanation: Positive second derivative = concave up = local minimum.

quiz.q: To find absolute extrema on [a,b], check:
quiz.explanation: Absolute extrema can occur at critical points inside the interval OR at the endpoints.

lessons.title: Mean Value Theorem & Rolle's Theorem
lessons.description: Understand and apply the Mean Value Theorem for derivatives.
lessons.formula:
MVT: If f continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b),
then f'(c) = [f(b)−f(a)]/(b−a) for some c in (a,b)

Rolle's: If f(a)=f(b), then f'(c)=0 for some c in (a,b)
lessons.content:
The Mean Value Theorem (MVT) guarantees that somewhere between two points on a differentiable curve, the instantaneous rate of change (tangent slope) equals the average rate of change (secant slope). Formally: there exists c in (a,b) where f'(c) = [f(b)−f(a)]/(b−a).

Rolle's Theorem is a special case: if f(a)=f(b), then there exists a point c where f'(c)=0 — the function must have a horizontal tangent somewhere in between.

The MVT is used to prove many important results in calculus, including inequalities and properties of derivatives.
steps: Verify f is continuous on [a,b]
Verify f is differentiable on (a,b)
Compute the average rate of change [f(b)−f(a)]/(b−a)
Set f'(x) = average rate of change
Solve for x to find the guaranteed point c

examples.title: MVT Application
examples.text: f(x)=x² on [1,3]. Average rate = (9−1)/(3−1) = 4. f'(x)=2x=4 → x=2. So c=2 is the MVT point.

examples.title: Rolle's Theorem
examples.text: f(x)=(x−1)(x−3) on [1,3]. f(1)=f(3)=0. f'(x)=2x−4=0→x=2. There is a critical point at x=2.

lessons.tip: The MVT says: somewhere on a road trip, your instantaneous speed equals your average speed. There must be at least one moment where the speedometer matches the overall average!

quiz.explanation: MVT: f'(c) = [f(b)−f(a)]/(b−a), which is the average rate of change.
Rolle's Theorem: if f(a)=f(b), then f'(c)=0 for some c in (a,b).

quiz.q: f(x)=x³ on [0,3]. MVT guarantees c where f'(c) = ?

options: f to be continuous and differentiable
f to have no critical points
quiz.explanation: MVT requires continuity on [a,b] and differentiability on (a,b).

lessons.title: Curve Sketching Using Derivatives
lessons.description: Use first and second derivatives to accurately sketch the graph of any function.
lessons.formula:
1st Derivative Test:
  f'(x) > 0 → function is increasing
  f'(x) < 0 → function is decreasing
  Critical points: where f'(x) = 0 or f'(x) is undefined

2nd Derivative Test:
  f''(x) > 0 → concave up (holds water)
  f''(x) < 0 → concave down (spills water)
  Inflection points: where f''(x) = 0 and changes sign

Local max: f'(c) = 0 and f''(c) < 0
Local min: f'(c) = 0 and f''(c) > 0
lessons.content:
Curve sketching is one of the most powerful applications of differential calculus. By combining information from the first and second derivatives, you can draw an accurate graph of virtually any function without plotting hundreds of points. The first derivative tells you where the function is increasing or decreasing, while the second derivative reveals concavity — whether the graph curves upward like a smile or downward like a frown.

The process begins by finding the domain of the function and any intercepts. Next, compute the first derivative and identify critical points — values where the derivative equals zero or is undefined. Use a sign chart for f'(x) to determine intervals of increase and decrease, and apply the First Derivative Test to classify each critical point as a local maximum, local minimum, or neither. Then compute the second derivative and find where f''(x) equals zero or is undefined to locate potential inflection points where concavity changes.

With all of this information assembled — domain, intercepts, critical points, intervals of monotonicity, concavity, and inflection points — you can sketch the graph step by step. Start by plotting the intercepts and critical points, then draw smooth curves that respect the increasing/decreasing and concave up/down behavior on each interval. This systematic approach produces accurate, professional-quality sketches that reveal the essential character of the function at a glance.
steps: Find the domain of the function and determine any asymptotes (vertical, horizontal, or slant).
Compute the first derivative f'(x), find critical points where f'(x) = 0 or is undefined, and build a sign chart for intervals of increase and decrease.
Compute the second derivative f''(x), find where f''(x) = 0 or is undefined, and determine concavity intervals using a sign chart for f''.
Identify inflection points where f''(x) changes sign, and classify critical points as local maxima or minima using the First or Second Derivative Test.
Plot all intercepts, critical points, and inflection points, then sketch the curve following the increasing/decreasing and concavity behavior on each interval.

examples.title: Sketch f(x) = x³ − 3x
examples.text: Step 1: Domain is all real numbers; y-intercept at (0,0), x-intercepts at x=0, ±√3. Step 2: f'(x) = 3x² − 3 = 3(x²−1), critical points at x = −1 and x = 1. Sign chart: f'(x) > 0 on (−∞,−1), f'(x) < 0 on (−1,1), f'(x) > 0 on (1,∞). So f has a local max at (−1,2) and a local min at (1,−2). Step 3: f''(x) = 6x, zero at x = 0. Concave down for x < 0, concave up for x > 0. Inflection point at (0,0). The graph is an S-shaped cubic passing through all three intercepts with a hill at x = −1 and a valley at x = 1.

examples.title: Identifying All Features of f(x) = x³ − 3x
examples.text: Summary of features: Domain: (−∞, ∞). y-intercept: (0,0). x-intercepts: (−√3, 0), (0,0), (√3, 0). Critical points: local maximum at (−1, 2) and local minimum at (1, −2). Intervals of increase: (−∞, −1) and (1, ∞). Interval of decrease: (−1, 1). Concave down on (−∞, 0), concave up on (0, ∞). Inflection point at (0, 0). End behavior: as x → −∞, f(x) → −∞; as x → ∞, f(x) → ∞. No asymptotes.

lessons.tip: Always find the domain first, then intercepts, then derivatives. A systematic order prevents missing features and ensures your sketch captures every important aspect of the function.

quiz.q: If f'(x) > 0 on an interval, the function is:
quiz.explanation: When the first derivative is positive, the function is increasing on that interval.

quiz.q: If f''(x) < 0 on an interval, the graph is:
quiz.explanation: A negative second derivative means the function is concave down (curves like a frown).

options: f''(x) = 0 and the concavity changes sign
quiz.explanation: An inflection point requires both f''(x) = 0 (or undefined) AND a change in concavity.

quiz.q: For f(x) = x³ − 3x, at x = 1 the function has:
quiz.explanation: f'(1) = 0 and f''(1) = 6 > 0, so by the Second Derivative Test there is a local minimum at x = 1.

lessons.title: Antiderivatives & Indefinite Integrals
lessons.description: Find functions whose derivatives are given — reverse differentiation.
lessons.formula:
∫x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C, n≠−1
∫1/x dx = ln|x| + C
∫e^x dx = e^x + C

Always add +C for indefinite integrals!
lessons.content:
An antiderivative of f(x) is a function F(x) whose derivative is f(x). The indefinite integral ∫f(x)dx represents ALL antiderivatives, differing only by a constant. This is why we always add +C.

The power rule for integration reverses the power rule for derivatives: ∫x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C (for n≠−1). Special cases: ∫1/x dx = ln|x| + C and ∫e^x dx = e^x + C.

Integration is fundamentally about 'undoing' differentiation. If F'(x) = f(x), then F is an antiderivative of f.
steps: Identify the integration rule needed
Apply the power rule or special formula
Always add +C
Check by differentiating your answer
If the integrand is complex, try simplifying first

examples.title: Power Rule
examples.text: ∫3x⁴ dx = 3·x⁵/5 + C = (3/5)x⁵ + C. Apply the power rule, then multiply by the coefficient.

examples.title: Special Cases
examples.text: ∫(2/x + 3e^x) dx = 2ln|x| + 3e^x + C. Use ln for 1/x and e^x integrates to itself.

lessons.tip: The +C is not optional! It represents an infinite family of functions, each shifted vertically by a different constant amount.

quiz.explanation: Power rule: x^(3+1)/(3+1) = x⁴/4 + C.
∫2x dx = 2·x²/2 + C = x² + C.
The exponential function is its own antiderivative: ∫e^x = e^x + C.
∫1/x dx = ln|x| + C. Absolute value ensures the domain includes negative x values.

lessons.title: Riemann Sums & Definite Integrals
lessons.description: Understand area approximation and the definite integral.
lessons.formula:
Definite Integral = lim(n→∞) Σ f(x_i*)Δx

∫(a→b) f(x)dx = F(b) − F(a)

Area = net signed area under the curve
lessons.content:
A Riemann sum approximates the area under a curve by dividing the region into thin rectangles. As the rectangles get thinner (n→∞), the approximation becomes exact — this limit is the definite integral.

The definite integral ∫(a→b) f(x)dx equals the net signed area between the curve and the x-axis. Area above the x-axis is positive; area below is negative. By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, ∫(a→b) f(x)dx = F(b) − F(a) where F is any antiderivative of f.
steps: Divide [a,b] into n equal subintervals of width Δx = (b−a)/n
Choose sample points (left, right, or midpoint)
Calculate the sum of f(x_i*)·Δx
Take the limit as n → ∞
Or use FTC: find antiderivative F, evaluate F(b)−F(a)
lessons.tip: The FTC is the bridge between differentiation and integration — it says these two 'opposite' operations are connected through evaluation at endpoints.

quiz.explanation: The definite integral equals the net signed area between the curve and x-axis.

lessons.title: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
lessons.description: Connect differentiation and integration through the FTC.
lessons.formula:
FTC Part 1:
d/dx [∫(a→x) f(t)dt] = f(x)

FTC Part 2:
∫(a→b) f(x)dx = F(b) − F(a)

where F'(x) = f(x)
lessons.content:
The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (FTC) is arguably the most important theorem in mathematics. It reveals that differentiation and integration are inverse operations — two sides of the same coin.

FTC Part 1 says: if f is continuous, then d/dx[∫(a→x) f(t)dt] = f(x). The derivative of the accumulation function gives back the original function.

FTC Part 2 says: ∫(a→b) f(x)dx = F(b) − F(a), where F is any antiderivative of f. This gives us a powerful method to evaluate definite integrals without computing Riemann sums.
steps: For FTC Part 2: find any antiderivative F of f
Evaluate F at the upper limit b
Evaluate F at the lower limit a
Subtract: F(b) − F(a)
For FTC Part 1: the derivative of an integral is just the integrand evaluated at the upper limit

examples.title: FTC Part 1
examples.text: d/dx[∫(2→x) t³ dt] = x³. By FTC Part 1, the derivative of the integral from 2 to x of t³ dt is simply x³.

lessons.tip: FTC Part 1 in plain English: 'The rate at which accumulated area changes equals the height of the function at that point.'

quiz.explanation: FTC Part 1: the derivative of ∫(a→x) f(t)dt = f(x). So the answer is e^x².
FTC Part 2: ∫(a→b) f(x)dx = F(b)−F(a) where F' = f.

lessons.title: Integration by Substitution (u-sub)
lessons.description: Use u-substitution to integrate composite functions.
lessons.formula:
u = g(x), du = g'(x)dx

∫f(g(x))·g'(x)dx = ∫f(u)du

Don't forget: if definite integral, change limits too!
lessons.content:
U-substitution is the integration counterpart of the chain rule. When the integrand contains a function and its derivative (or part of it), we substitute u = inner function to simplify.

The key is recognizing when u-substitution applies: look for a 'function of a function' where the derivative of the inner function appears (perhaps multiplied by a constant).

For definite integrals, you can either substitute back to x before evaluating, or change the limits to u-values and evaluate directly — both give the same answer.
steps: Identify the inner function g(x) — set u = g(x)
Find du = g'(x)dx
Substitute u and du into the integral
Integrate with respect to u
Substitute back x = g⁻¹(u) (or change limits for definite integrals)

examples.title: Basic u-sub
examples.text: ∫2x(x²+1)³ dx. Let u=x²+1, du=2x dx. Integral becomes ∫u³ du = u⁴/4 + C = (x²+1)⁴/4 + C.

examples.title: Definite integral
examples.text: ∫(0→1) 2x·e^(x²) dx. Let u=x², du=2x dx. Limits: 0→0, 1→1. ∫(0→1) e^u du = e^1 − e^0 = e−1.

lessons.tip: Choose u so that du appears (up to a constant) in the integrand. If you have to work hard to find du, try a different substitution!

quiz.explanation: u=x², du=2x dx. ∫cos u du = sin u + C = sin(x²)+C.
If u-substitution doesn't simplify the integral, try integration by parts or other techniques.
u=1+e^x, du=e^x dx. ∫1/u du = ln|u|+C = ln(1+e^x)+C.

lessons.title: Area Between Curves
lessons.description: Calculate the area between two functions using integrals.
lessons.formula:
Area = ∫(a→b) [f(x) − g(x)] dx

where f(x) ≥ g(x) on [a,b]

Find intersection points: set f(x) = g(x)
lessons.content:
The area between two curves f(x) and g(x) from x=a to x=b is found by integrating the difference of the functions: ∫(a→b) [f(x)−g(x)] dx. Always subtract the lower curve from the upper curve to get a positive result.

First find the intersection points by setting f(x)=g(x) — these determine the limits of integration. If the curves cross, split the integral at the crossing point and integrate each region separately.
steps: Set f(x) = g(x) to find intersection points
Determine which function is on top in each region
Set up the integral: ∫[top − bottom] dx
Evaluate the definite integral
The result is the area (always positive)

examples.title: Area Between Lines and Curve
examples.text: Area between y=x² and y=x from x=0 to x=1: ∫(0→1) [x−x²] dx = [x²/2−x³/3](0→1) = 1/2−1/3 = 1/6.

examples.title: Curves That Cross
examples.text: Area between y=x and y=x³ from x=−1 to x=1: ∫(−1→0) [x−x³]dx + ∫(0→1) [x³−x]dx. Top function switches at x=0!

lessons.tip: Sketch the graphs! Knowing which curve is on top in each region prevents sign errors in your integral.

quiz.q: Area between y=x² and y=x (x from 0 to 1):

quiz.explanation: Area = ∫[top function − bottom function] dx.

quiz.q: Intersection points of y=x² and y=4:
quiz.explanation: x²=4 → x=±2. Intersection points at (−2,4) and (2,4).

quiz.q: Area between y=√x and y=x from 0 to 1:

lessons.title: Introduction to Differential Equations
lessons.description: Understand what differential equations are and solve basic separable equations.
lessons.formula:
Separable: dy/dx = f(x)g(y)
1. Separate: dy/g(y) = f(x)dx
2. Integrate both sides
3. Solve for y
4. Apply initial condition if given
lessons.content:
A differential equation relates a function to its derivatives. The simplest type is a separable equation dy/dx = f(x)·g(y), where we can separate the variables and integrate both sides.

The order of a differential equation is the highest derivative that appears. A slope field (direction field) is a graphical representation showing the slope at many points, giving a picture of all possible solution curves.

When an initial condition is given, we can find the particular solution (not just the general solution family) by solving for the constant C.
steps: Verify the equation is separable
Separate variables: get all y terms with dy, all x terms with dx
Integrate both sides
Add +C to one side
Apply the initial condition to find C

examples.title: Basic Separable
