examples.text: dy/dx = x/y. Separate: y dy = x dx. Integrate: y²/2 = x²/2 + C. y² = x² + C.

examples.title: With Initial Condition
examples.text: dy/dx = 2x, y(0)=3. dy = 2x dx. y = x² + C. 3 = 0 + C → C=3. y = x²+3.

lessons.tip: Separation of variables is like algebraically 'sorting' the equation — all y's on one side, all x's on the other, then integrate.

quiz.explanation: dy/y = dx. ln|y| = x + C. y = e^(x+C) = Ce^x.
Can separate as y dy = x dx, so it is separable.
Slope fields draw small line segments showing the slope dy/dx at each point.

quiz.q: The order of dy/dx + y = 0 is:
quiz.explanation: The highest derivative is the first derivative, so order = 1.

lessons.title: Slope Fields & Solution Curves
lessons.description: Draw and interpret slope fields for first-order differential equations.
lessons.formula:
Slope Field:
At each point (x,y), draw a short segment with slope dy/dx

Equilibrium: dy/dx = 0 → horizontal segments

Euler's Method:
y(n+1) = y(n) + f(x(n),y(n)) · Δx
lessons.content:
A slope field (direction field) visualizes a differential equation by drawing short line segments at grid points, each with slope equal to dy/dx at that point. Solution curves follow the slope field — they are tangent to every segment they pass through.

Equilibrium solutions occur where dy/dx = 0 everywhere, producing horizontal lines. These are constant solutions where the function doesn't change.

Euler's method is a numerical technique to approximate solution curves: starting from an initial point, follow the slope field step by step.
steps: Choose a grid of (x,y) points
At each point, compute dy/dx
Draw a short segment with that slope
Equilibrium solutions appear as horizontal lines
Solution curves thread through the field following the slopes

examples.title: Identifying Equilibrium
examples.text: dy/dx = y−3. Equilibrium when y−3=0, so y=3 is the equilibrium solution.

lessons.tip: Slope fields are like 'gravitational fields' for differential equations — the solution curves are like objects flowing along the field lines.

quiz.explanation: Equilibrium means dy/dx = 0, so all segments are horizontal.

quiz.q: In a slope field for dy/dx = x, slopes:
quiz.explanation: dy/dx = x: the slope depends only on the x-coordinate.
Euler's method approximates solutions by taking small steps along the slope field.
y(1−y)=0 when y=0 or y=1. Both are equilibrium solutions.

lessons.title: AP Calculus AB Exam Tips & Strategies
lessons.description: Essential tips, common mistakes, and strategies for the AP exam.
lessons.formula:
AP Calculus AB Exam Structure:
Section 1: 30 MC (60 min, no calculator)
Section 2: 15 MC + 3 FRQ (45 min, calculator)
Section 3: 3 FRQ (60 min, no calculator)

Total: 3 hours 15 minutes
lessons.content:
The AP Calculus AB exam tests your understanding of limits, derivatives, integrals, and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. It consists of multiple-choice and free-response sections, some with and without a calculator.

Key strategies: show all your work on FRQs (partial credit!), check units in word problems, verify answers make sense, and manage your time carefully. The most tested topics are the Fundamental Theorem, related rates, and optimization.

Common mistakes include forgetting +C on indefinite integrals, incorrect chain rule applications, and not checking endpoints in optimization problems.
steps: Master the core rules: power, product, quotient, chain
Practice FTC problems — they appear everywhere
Show all work on FRQs for partial credit
Check answers for reasonableness
Time yourself during practice exams

examples.title: FRQ Strategy
examples.text: Even if you can't solve the whole problem, solve parts you know. Partial credit on each sub-part. Label everything clearly.

examples.title: Calculator vs No-Calculator
examples.text: Know which rules to apply by hand. Use the calculator only for numeric evaluation, graphing, and checking.

lessons.tip: The most valuable exam skill: knowing when you can use a calculator vs. when you must show the analytical work. Misusing the calculator on a no-calculator section costs points!

quiz.q: The AP Calculus AB exam is how long?
quiz.explanation: The total exam time is 3 hours and 15 minutes.
FRQ = Free Response Question. These require you to show your work and reasoning.

options: Show all work for partial credit
Skip problems you can't fully solve
quiz.explanation: Always show all your work! You earn partial credit for correct steps even if the final answer is wrong.

quiz.q: The most tested topic on the AP exam is:
quiz.explanation: FTC problems appear on nearly every AP Calculus exam in both MC and FRQ formats.

lessons.title: L'Hôpital's Rule
lessons.description: Apply L'Hôpital's Rule to evaluate limits of indeterminate forms 0/0 and ∞/∞
lessons.formula:
L'Hôpital's Rule:
If lim f(x)/g(x) gives 0/0 or ∞/∞, then:
lim f(x)/g(x) = lim f'(x)/g'(x)

Indeterminate Forms:
0/0, ∞/∞, 0·∞, ∞−∞, 0⁰, 1^∞, ∞⁰

For 0·∞: rewrite as 0/(1/∞) or ∞/(1/0)
For 1^∞: use y = e^(ln·f·g)
lessons.content:
L'Hôpital's Rule is a powerful technique for evaluating limits that produce indeterminate forms (0/0 or ∞/∞). When direct substitution gives one of these forms, take the derivative of the numerator and denominator separately and try the limit again. You can apply the rule multiple times if needed.

The rule works ONLY for 0/0 or ∞/∞ forms. For other indeterminate forms (like 0·∞, 1∞, or ∞−∞), you must first algebraically rewrite the expression into one of the two standard forms. Always verify the indeterminate form before applying—otherwise you may get incorrect answers!
steps: Verify the limit produces 0/0 or ∞/∞ by direct substitution
If yes, differentiate the numerator and denominator separately
Re-evaluate the limit with the new expressions
If still indeterminate, apply L'Hôpital's Rule again
If the limit evaluates to a number, that is the answer

examples.title: Evaluating 0/0
examples.text: lim(x→0) sin(x)/x = 0/0. Apply L'Hôpital: lim cos(x)/1 = cos(0) = 1. This confirms the famous limit sin(x)/x → 1 as x → 0.

examples.title: Applying Twice
examples.text: lim(x→∞) x²/e^x = ∞/∞. First: lim 2x/e^x = ∞/∞. Second: lim 2/e^x = 2/∞ = 0. Exponential growth always wins over polynomials!

lessons.tip: L'Hôpital's Rule is NOT the quotient rule! You differentiate numerator and denominator separately, not as a quotient. Also, always CHECK that you have 0/0 or ∞/∞ before applying—if you get 5/0, the limit is already ±∞, not indeterminate!

quiz.explanation: Direct sub gives 0/0. Apply L'Hôpital: e^x/1 at x=0 = e⁰ = 1.

quiz.q: Can L'Hôpital's Rule be applied to lim(x→2) (x²−4)/(x−2)?
quiz.explanation: Direct: 0/0. Apply: (2x)/1 at x=2 = 4. So lim = 4.

quiz.q: If applying L'Hôpital's Rule once still gives ∞/∞, what should you do?
quiz.explanation: You can apply L'Hôpital's Rule repeatedly as long as each step produces 0/0 or ∞/∞.

lessons.title: Derivatives of Exponential and Logarithmic Functions
lessons.description: Find derivatives of eˣ, ln(x), aˣ, and log_a(x)
lessons.formula:
Key Derivatives:
d/dx[e^x] = e^x
d/dx[ln x] = 1/x
d/dx[a^x] = a^x · ln a
d/dx[log_a x] = 1/(x · ln a)

Chain Rule Forms:
d/dx[e^(u)] = e^(u) · u'
d/dx[ln(u)] = u'/u
d/dx[a^(u)] = a^(u) · ln a · u'
lessons.content:
The derivative of ex is itself—ex—making it the most elegant function in calculus. The derivative of ln(x) is 1/x. These are foundational results that appear everywhere in applications. For other bases, the chain rule introduces the natural log of the base as a scaling factor.

Logarithmic differentiation is a technique for differentiating complicated products and quotients: take the natural log of both sides, then differentiate implicitly. This converts products into sums and powers into multipliers, often simplifying difficult derivatives dramatically. Remember that d/dx[ln|u|] = u'/u works for negative u too.
steps: Identify the base: is it e, or another base a?
If e: d/dx[e^(u)] = e^(u) · u' using the chain rule
If a: d/dx[a^(u)] = a^(u) · ln(a) · u'
For logarithms: d/dx[ln(u)] = u'/u
For log base a: d/dx[log_a(u)] = u'/(u · ln a)

examples.title: Derivative of e^(3x²+1)
examples.text: d/dx[e^(3x²+1)] = e^(3x²+1) · d/dx(3x²+1) = e^(3x²+1) · 6x = 6x · e^(3x²+1). The exponential stays, multiply by the inner derivative.

examples.title: Logarithmic Differentiation
examples.text: y = x^x. Take ln: ln y = x ln x. Differentiate: y'/y = 1·ln(x) + x·(1/x) = ln(x) + 1. So y' = x^x(ln x + 1). Neither power rule nor exponential rule works alone here!

lessons.tip: The key insight: e^x is its own derivative! This makes it the 'identity function' of differentiation. For a^x, the extra ln(a) factor appears because a^x = e^(x ln a), and the chain rule brings out ln(a).

quiz.explanation: d/dx[e^(5x)] = e^(5x) · 5 = 5e^(5x) by the chain rule.
d/dx[ln(u)] = u'/u. u = x²+1, u' = 2x. Result: 2x/(x²+1).
d/dx[a^x] = a^x · ln a. So d/dx[3^x] = 3^x · ln 3.

lessons.title: Optimization Word Problems
lessons.description: Solve real-world optimization problems using derivatives and critical points
lessons.formula:
Optimization Steps:
1. Define variables and objective function
2. Write the constraint equation
3. Express objective in one variable
4. Find derivative and set = 0
5. Classify critical points

First Derivative Test:
f'(x) changes + to − at c → local max
f'(x) changes − to + at c → local min

Second Derivative Test:
f''(c) < 0 → local max
f''(c) > 0 → local min
lessons.content:
Optimization finds the maximum or minimum value of a quantity subject to constraints. The process: define variables, write the objective function (what you want to optimize), use constraints to reduce to one variable, find critical points by setting the derivative to zero, then classify each point as a maximum or minimum.

Real-world applications include maximizing area with a fixed perimeter (fencing problems), minimizing material for a given volume (packaging), maximizing profit or revenue, and minimizing travel time. Always verify endpoints of the domain—the extreme value theorem guarantees that continuous functions on closed intervals attain their max and min values either at critical points or at endpoints.
steps: Read the problem carefully and identify what to maximize/minimize
Define variables and write the objective function
Use constraints to express the objective in one variable
Find the derivative and set it equal to zero to find critical points
Verify the answer: check second derivative or evaluate the function at critical points and endpoints

examples.title: Maximizing Area
examples.text: 120 ft of fencing for a rectangular garden against a wall. Width x, length (120−2x). Area A = x(120−2x) = 120x − 2x². A' = 120−4x = 0 → x = 30. A'' = −4 < 0 (max). Max area: 30×60 = 1800 ft².

examples.title: Minimizing Cost
examples.text: Cylindrical can with volume 500π cm³. Minimize surface area. V = πr²h = 500π, h = 500/r². SA = 2πr² + 2πr(500/r²) = 2πr² + 1000π/r. SA' = 4πr − 1000π/r² = 0 → r = 5. h = 20. Min SA = 300π cm².

lessons.tip: Always check your answer makes sense! If you find a 'maximum' area of −500 square feet, something is wrong. Also, endpoints of the domain can give the actual max/min even if the derivative is never zero there!

quiz.q: A farmer has 200 ft of fencing. What dimensions maximize the rectangular area?
quiz.explanation: For a rectangle with fixed perimeter, a square maximizes area. 200/4 = 50 ft per side.

quiz.q: To confirm a critical point is a maximum, which test can you use?
quiz.explanation: f'(x) going from positive to negative means f increases then decreases, indicating a local maximum.

quiz.q: In optimization, what is the constraint?
options: A condition that limits the variables
quiz.explanation: The constraint is a condition (equation) relating the variables, such as 'total fencing = 200 ft.'

lessons.title: Related Rates Word Problems
lessons.description: Solve related rates problems involving changing quantities
lessons.formula:
Related Rates Steps:
1. Draw a diagram and label variables
2. Write the equation relating the quantities
3. Differentiate BOTH sides with respect to time t
4. Substitute known values and solve for unknown rate
5. Include units in the answer

Chain Rule for Time:
d/dt[f(g(t))] = f'(g(t)) · g'(t)

Key: every variable is a function of time!
d/dt[x²] = 2x · dx/dt
lessons.content:
Related rates problems involve finding how fast one quantity changes when you know how fast a related quantity changes. The key is to write an equation connecting the quantities, then differentiate both sides with respect to time t using the chain rule. Every variable that changes with time gets a dx/dt term.

Common related rates scenarios include: a ladder sliding down a wall (Pythagorean theorem), a balloon being inflated (volume of a sphere), two cars moving apart (distance formula), a cone filling with water (volume of a cone), and shadows changing length (similar triangles). Always draw a diagram, identify what's given and what's asked, and differentiate carefully. Remember to substitute known values AFTER differentiating!
steps: Draw a diagram and label all variables with their current values
Write an equation relating the quantities (geometry, physics formulas)
Differentiate both sides with respect to time t (every variable becomes a rate)
Substitute all known values for the variables AND their rates
Solve for the unknown rate and include units

examples.title: Sliding Ladder
examples.text: 10-ft ladder against wall. Bottom slides at 2 ft/s. How fast is top sliding when bottom is 6 ft out? x²+y²=100. Differentiate: 2x(dx/dt)+2y(dy/dt)=0. At x=6: y=8. 2(6)(2)+2(8)(dy/dt)=0. dy/dt = −24/16 = −1.5 ft/s (falling).

examples.title: Expanding Circle
examples.text: Ripple radius grows at 3 cm/s. How fast does area grow when r = 5? A = πr². dA/dt = 2πr(dr/dt) = 2π(5)(3) = 30π cm²/s. Area grows at 30π cm²/s.

lessons.tip: CRITICAL: Substitute known values AFTER differentiating, not before! If you substitute r = 5 before differentiating A = πr², you get dA/dt = 0 (wrong!). Differentiate first to get dA/dt = 2πr(dr/dt), then substitute.

quiz.q: A sphere's radius grows at 2 cm/s. When r = 5, how fast does volume grow?
quiz.explanation: V = (4/3)πr³. dV/dt = 4πr²(dr/dt) = 4π(25)(2) = 200π... Wait, 4π×25×2 = 200π. Hmm, let me recalculate: 4π(25)(2) = 200π. Answer is B.

quiz.q: When should you substitute known values in related rates?
options: Only at the end of the problem
quiz.explanation: Always differentiate first, then substitute. Substituting too early eliminates variables you need to differentiate.

quiz.q: Two cars leave an intersection. One goes north at 60 mph, the other east at 80 mph. How fast is the distance between them changing after 2 hours?

lessons.title: Euler's Method
lessons.description: Approximate solutions to differential equations using Euler's Method
lessons.formula:
Euler's Method:
y_(n+1) = y_n + h · f(x_n, y_n)

Where:
  h = step size (Δx)
  f(x, y) = dy/dx (the slope)
  (x₀, y₀) = initial condition

Repeat:
x_(n+1) = x_n + h
Compute slope at (x_n, y_n)
y_(n+1) = y_n + h · slope

Accuracy improves with smaller h
lessons.content:
Euler's Method is a numerical technique for approximating solutions to differential equations when an exact solution is difficult or impossible to find. Starting from an initial condition, it follows the tangent line at each point to estimate the next point, stepping forward in small increments.

Given dy/dx = f(x, y) with initial condition y(x0) = y0, the method uses the slope f(xn, yn) at each step to project forward: yn+1 = yn + h · f(xn, yn). The step size h controls accuracy: smaller h gives better approximations but requires more computation. Euler's Method is the simplest numerical ODE solver and the foundation for more advanced methods like Runge-Kutta.
steps: Identify the differential equation dy/dx = f(x, y) and initial condition (x₀, y₀)
Choose the step size h and the number of steps
Compute the slope at the current point: m = f(x_n, y_n)
Update: y_(n+1) = y_n + h · m and x_(n+1) = x_n + h
Repeat until reaching the desired x-value

examples.title: Effect of Step Size
examples.text: Same equation, h = 0.25. More steps but better accuracy. With h=0.25: y(0.25)=1.125, y(0.5)=1.328, y(0.75)=1.582, y(1.0)=1.891. Compare with h=0.5 giving y(1.0)=2.5. Smaller step = more accurate!

lessons.tip: Think of Euler's Method as 'walk along the slope field.' At each point, you check the slope and walk in that direction for a small step. The approximation gets better with smaller steps, like following a curve more closely with smaller straight-line segments.

quiz.q: Given dy/dx = 2x, y(0) = 3, h = 0.1. What is y(0.1)?
quiz.explanation: slope = 2(0) = 0. y(0.1) = 3 + 0.1(0) = 3.0. The slope is 0 at x=0, so y doesn't change in this first step.

quiz.q: What happens to accuracy when you decrease the step size h?
quiz.explanation: Smaller step size means following the curve more closely with smaller straight segments, improving accuracy.

quiz.q: Euler's Method approximates solutions by following what?
quiz.explanation: Euler's Method uses the tangent line (slope) at each point to estimate the next point, creating a piecewise linear approximation.

lessons.title: Separation of Variables
lessons.description: Solve first-order differential equations using separation of variables
lessons.formula:
Separation of Variables:
If dy/dx = f(x) · g(y), then:
1/g(y) dy = f(x) dx
2. Integrate both sides
3. ∫ 1/g(y) dy = ∫ f(x) dx
4. Add constant of integration C
5. Solve for y if possible

If given initial condition:
Substitute to find C
This gives the particular solution
lessons.content:
Separation of variables is a technique for solving first-order differential equations where the derivative dy/dx can be expressed as a product of a function of x and a function of y. The method rearranges the equation so all y terms (with dy) are on one side and all x terms (with dx) are on the other, then integrates both sides.

The solution always includes an integration constant C. If an initial condition is given, substitute to find C and obtain the particular solution. Without an initial condition, the solution is a general solution representing a family of curves. This method works for equations like dy/dx = xy (separable as dy/y = x dx), dy/dx = ex/y, and population growth dy/dt = ky.
steps: Verify the equation is separable: dy/dx = f(x) · g(y)
Separate: move all y terms (with dy) to one side, x terms (with dx) to the other
Integrate both sides
Add the constant of integration C
If an initial condition is given, substitute to find C

examples.title: Solving dy/dx = xy
examples.text: Separate: dy/y = x dx. Integrate: ln|y| = x²/2 + C. Solve: y = Ce^(x²/2). If y(0) = 3: 3 = Ce⁰ = C. Particular solution: y = 3e^(x²/2).

examples.title: Exponential Growth DE
examples.text: dy/dt = 0.05y. Separate: dy/y = 0.05 dt. Integrate: ln|y| = 0.05t + C. y = Ce^(0.05t). If y(0) = 100: y = 100e^(0.05t). Classic exponential growth!

lessons.tip: Not all DEs are separable! Check: can you write it as f(y)dy = g(x)dx? If variables are mixed (like dy/dx = x+y), separation of variables won't work directly. The test: can you algebraically put all x's with dx on one side and all y's with dy on the other?

quiz.explanation: Separate: y dy = x dx. Integrate: y²/2 = x²/2 + C. Multiply by 2: y² = x² + C.

quiz.q: dy/dx = 2x with y(0) = 5. Find the particular solution.
quiz.explanation: dy = 2x dx. Integrate: y = x² + C. y(0)=5: 5 = 0 + C. So y = x² + 5.

quiz.q: Which differential equation is NOT separable?
quiz.explanation: dy/dx = x + y cannot be written as f(x)g(y). The sum x+y prevents separation.

lessons.title: Particle Motion
lessons.description: Analyze position, velocity, and acceleration of particles in motion
lessons.formula:
Relationships:
s(t) = position
v(t) = s'(t) = ds/dt (velocity)
a(t) = v'(t) = dv/dt (acceleration)

Displacement:
Δs = s(b) − s(a)

Total Distance:
∫|v(t)| dt from a to b

Speed = |v(t)|
Speeding up when v and a have same sign
Slowing down when v and a have opposite signs
lessons.content:
Particle motion on a line is a key application of derivatives and integrals. The position function s(t) gives location at time t. The velocity v(t) = s'(t) tells you speed and direction. The acceleration a(t) = v'(t) tells you how velocity is changing.

When v(t) > 0, the particle moves right (forward). When v(t) < 0, it moves left (backward). Setting v(t) = 0 finds turning points where the particle changes direction. Displacement is s(b) − s(a), which can be negative. Total distance traveled is the integral of |v(t)|, which is always positive. A particle speeds up when velocity and acceleration have the same sign and slows down when they have opposite signs.
steps: Find velocity: v(t) = s'(t) by differentiating position
Find acceleration: a(t) = v'(t) by differentiating velocity
Set v(t) = 0 to find when the particle changes direction
Calculate displacement: s(b) − s(a)
Calculate total distance: integrate |v(t)| between critical points

examples.title: Analyzing Motion
examples.text: s(t) = t³ − 6t² + 9t. v(t) = 3t² − 12t + 9 = 3(t−1)(t−3). v(t)=0 at t=1,3. v>0 for t<1 (moving right), v<0 for 1<t<3 (left), v>0 for t>3 (right). Particle turns at t=1 and t=3.

examples.title: Displacement vs Total Distance
examples.text: v(t) = t² − 4 from t=0 to t=3. Displacement = ∫(t²−4)dt = [t³/3−4t]₀³ = 9−12 = −3. But total distance = ∫|t²−4|dt must split at t=2 where v=0. = 16/3 + 1/3 = 17/3.

lessons.tip: Displacement can be NEGATIVE (net change), but total distance is always POSITIVE. Always check if the particle changes direction between the time bounds—if so, you must split the integral at the turning point!

quiz.q: If s(t) = 2t² − 8t + 3, when is the particle at rest?
quiz.explanation: v(t) = 4t − 8. Set v = 0: 4t − 8 = 0, t = 2. The particle is at rest at t = 2.

quiz.q: A particle moves right when v(t) is...
quiz.explanation: Positive velocity means the particle moves in the positive direction (right on a number line).
Total distance is the integral of the absolute value of velocity, accounting for direction changes.

lessons.title: FTC Applications
lessons.description: Apply the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus to evaluate definite integrals and find areas
lessons.formula:
Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (Part 2):
∫[a to b] f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a)
where F'(x) = f(x)

FTC Part 1:
d/dx [∫[a to x] f(t) dt] = f(x)

Area Between Curves:
A = ∫[a to b] |f(x) − g(x)| dx
  = ∫[a to b] (top − bottom) dx

Net Change Theorem:
∫[a to b] F'(x) dx = F(b) − F(a)
lessons.content:
The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (FTC) connects differentiation and integration, the two central operations in calculus. Part 2 states that a definite integral can be evaluated by finding any antiderivative and plugging in the bounds: ∫ab f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a). Part 1 states that the derivative of an integral function is the original integrand.

Key applications include: finding area between curves (integrate top minus bottom), computing net change (displacement from velocity), calculating accumulated quantities (total water in a tank, total charge), and determining average value of a function. The integral gives the NET signed area—areas above the x-axis count positive, below count negative.
steps: For definite integrals: find the antiderivative F(x)
Evaluate F(b) − F(a)
For area between curves: identify which function is on top
Integrate (top − bottom) from a to b
For accumulation: interpret the integral as total change from the rate function

examples.title: Area Between Curves
examples.text: Area between y = x² and y = x from x=0 to x=1. Top: y=x, Bottom: y=x². A = ∫[0 to 1] (x − x²) dx = [x²/2 − x³/3]₀¹ = (1/2 − 1/3) = 1/6.

lessons.tip: The FTC is the bridge between the two halves of calculus: derivatives and integrals. Think of it as: the integral 'undoes' the derivative and vice versa. F(b) − F(a) measures the net accumulated change from a to b.

quiz.explanation: ∫ 3x² dx = x³. Evaluate from 0 to 2: 2³ − 0³ = 8.

quiz.q: FTC Part 1 says d/dx[∫[0 to x] sin(t) dt] = ?
quiz.explanation: By FTC Part 1, the derivative of the integral from a constant to x of f(t) dt is simply f(x) = sin(x).
The definite integral gives net signed area: positive above the x-axis, negative below.

lessons.title: Review: Key Theorems
lessons.description: Review the IVT, EVT, MVT, and FTC and their applications
lessons.formula:
Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT):
If f is continuous on [a, b] and
N is between f(a) and f(b),
then f(c) = N for some c in (a, b).

Extreme Value Theorem (EVT):
If f is continuous on [a, b],
f attains absolute max and min on [a, b].

Mean Value Theorem (MVT):
If f is continuous on [a, b] and
differentiable on (a, b), then
f'(c) = [f(b)−f(a)]/(b−a) for some c in (a,b).

Rolle's Theorem:
If f(a)=f(b), then f'(c)=0 for some c in (a,b).
lessons.content:
The major theorems of calculus provide the theoretical foundation for the entire subject. The Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT) guarantees that a continuous function takes every value between f(a) and f(b)—essential for proving equations have solutions. The Extreme Value Theorem (EVT) guarantees that continuous functions on closed intervals always have a maximum and minimum.

The Mean Value Theorem (MVT) states there exists a point where the instantaneous rate of change equals the average rate of change—geometrically, some tangent line is parallel to the secant line. Rolle's Theorem is a special case: if f(a) = f(b), there exists a point where f'(c) = 0. The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (FTC) links differentiation and integration. Together, these theorems justify the methods we use in calculus.
steps: Identify which theorem applies to the given situation
For IVT: verify continuity on [a,b] and that the target value is between f(a) and f(b)
For EVT: verify continuity on a closed interval [a,b]
For MVT: verify continuity on [a,b] and differentiability on (a,b), then find average rate
For FTC: find the antiderivative and evaluate at bounds

examples.title: Using IVT to Prove a Root
examples.text: f(x) = x³ − x − 1. f(1) = −1, f(2) = 5. Since f is continuous and −1 < 0 < 5, IVT guarantees f(c) = 0 for some c in (1, 2). There is a real root between 1 and 2.

examples.title: Applying MVT
examples.text: f(x) = x² on [1, 3]. Average rate: [f(3)−f(1)]/(3−1) = (9−1)/2 = 4. MVT: f'(c) = 2c = 4, so c = 2. Indeed, the tangent at x=2 has slope 4, equal to the secant slope.

lessons.tip: Remember the hierarchy: Rolle's Theorem is a special case of MVT (when f(a)=f(b)), and MVT is the big brother that applies more generally. IVT is about values the function takes; EVT is about max/min; MVT is about rates of change.

quiz.q: Which theorem guarantees f(x) = xµ + x has a real root?
quiz.explanation: f(−1) = −2 < 0 and f(1) = 2 > 0. By IVT, since f is continuous, there exists c where f(c) = 0.
MVT says f'(c) = [f(b)−f(a)]/(b−a), the average rate of change equals some instantaneous rate.

quiz.q: EVT requires the function to be what on a closed interval?
quiz.explanation: EVT requires continuity on a closed interval [a,b] to guarantee absolute max and min exist.
